title.raw: 41A Notice (Section 35 BNSS) from the Police — What It Means and What to Do
title.rendered: 41A Notice (Section 35 BNSS) from the Police — What It Means and What to Do

content.raw:
In short

For offences punishable with imprisonment of up to seven years, the police are generally expected to issue a notice of appearance under Section 35(3) BNSS (the old Section 41A CrPC) instead of arresting. A person who complies with the notice is not to be arrested for that offence unless the police record reasons why arrest has become necessary. Failing to comply can lead to arrest. If the case involves offences punishable with more than seven years, or there is a real risk of arrest, an anticipatory bail application should be considered before appearing.

What to do when you receive the notice

  1. Read the notice carefully — the FIR number, sections, police station, date and time of appearance.
  2. Get a copy of the FIR (usually available online or from the police station) and check the maximum punishment for every section applied.
  3. Consult an advocate before you appear, especially if any section carries more than seven years, or if co-accused have been arrested.
  4. Appear on the date, or seek a new date in writing with reasons. Keep proof of every communication.
  5. Carry documents the notice asks for, and identity proof. Answer questions truthfully; you are not obliged to incriminate yourself.

Can I be arrested after appearing?

Where a person complies with the notice, arrest requires the police to record reasons. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that arrest in offences punishable up to seven years should not be routine. For offences punishable with less than three years, where the person is infirm or above 60 years of age, arrest needs the prior permission of an officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police (Section 35(7) BNSS).

When anticipatory bail is still advisable

  • Any section in the FIR is punishable with more than seven years (for example, cheating of a large amount, or offences under special laws).
  • Co-accused in the same FIR have been arrested.
  • The police are seeking recovery of money, documents or devices.
  • The matter is with the Economic Offences Wing, cyber police or a special unit.

  • How anticipatory bail works in Pune
  • Cyber police notice — first 72 hours
  • EOW and financial-crime matters

Section 35 BNSS is the new Section 41A CrPC

Since 1 July 2024, the 41A notice is issued under Section 35(3) of the BNSS. The content is the same: a notice to appear before the police instead of being arrested. Sections 35(4) to 35(6) set out the duty to comply, the protection from arrest on compliance, and the consequence of not complying.

41A / Section 35 notice in 498A, POCSO, SC/ST and cyber cases

  • 498A (cruelty) cases: the Supreme Court’s directions in Arnesh Kumar require the police to follow the notice procedure rather than arrest routinely.
  • POCSO and SC/ST Act cases: many offences carry more than seven years, or special provisions apply, so the notice route may not be available — take advice before appearing.
  • Cyber crime: Pune’s cyber police commonly issue notices to persons linked to accounts, numbers or devices under investigation.

Can a Section 35 notice be issued without an FIR?

A notice under Section 35 relates to a cognizable offence of which the person is reasonably suspected — usually after an FIR or a complaint under enquiry. A phone call or WhatsApp message asking you to come to the police station should be verified: ask for the FIR or enquiry number and the section under which you are being called.

title.raw: Default Bail & Undertrial Release (S.187 & S.479 BNSS)
title.rendered: Default Bail & Undertrial Release (S.187 & S.479 BNSS)

content.raw:
In short

Default bail: if the police do not file the charge-sheet within 60 days of remand (or 90 days for offences punishable with death, life imprisonment or imprisonment of ten years or more), the accused is entitled to bail under Section 187(3) BNSS — but only if the application is made before the charge-sheet is filed. Undertrial release: under Section 479 BNSS, an undertrial who has been detained for half the maximum sentence for the offence — or one-third for a first-time offender — is to be released on bail, except in offences punishable with death or life imprisonment.

Default bail — how the right works

  • The 60/90 days are counted from the date of the first remand order by the Magistrate.
  • The right is indefeasible once the period expires and the accused applies and is ready to furnish bail — the police cannot defeat it by filing the charge-sheet afterwards.
  • If the accused does not apply in time and the charge-sheet is filed, the right is lost, and bail has to be argued on merits.
  • Special laws can extend the period (for example, NDPS cases where the court extends time on the Public Prosecutor’s report, or UAPA). Whether an extension was validly granted is often the real issue.
  • An incomplete charge-sheet filed only to defeat default bail can itself be challenged.

Section 479 — release after long custody

  • Half of the maximum sentence served as an undertrial → release on bail.
  • First-time offender (no previous conviction) → release after one-third of the maximum sentence.
  • Not available for offences punishable with death or life imprisonment, or where the person faces cases in more than one offence in which investigation or trial is pending.
  • The jail superintendent is required to apply to the court once the period is complete, but families should not wait — an application can be filed directly.

When neither applies: long custody as a ground on merits

Even where the charge-sheet is filed on time and the offence is serious, prolonged custody with a trial that is not progressing — few witnesses examined, charges not framed — is weighed by courts under Article 21. Our reported orders include notes on orders granting bail after three to four years in custody.

  • Police custody and remand
  • Bail rejected at Sessions Court — what next

Default bail meaning, in simple words

Default bail — also called statutory bail — is bail the accused gets because the police defaulted: they did not file the chargesheet within the time the law allows. It does not depend on the merits of the case. Simple Hinglish mein: chargesheet time-limit ke andar file na ho, to milne wali bail.

Default bail in NDPS, POCSO and UAPA cases

LawTime to file chargesheet
Ordinary offences (BNSS)60 days; 90 days for offences punishable with death, life imprisonment or 10+ years
NDPS Act (certain offences)180 days, extendable up to one year on the Public Prosecutor’s report (Section 36A(4))
POCSO ActThe ordinary 60/90-day rule applies
UAPA90 days, extendable up to 180 days on the Public Prosecutor’s report

Can default bail be cancelled or rejected?

Default bail is not cancelled merely because the chargesheet is filed afterwards; it may be cancelled on grounds such as misuse of liberty. An application is rejected if it is made only after the chargesheet has been filed, or if the period was lawfully extended under a special law.

Undertrials in Yerawada: who applies under Section 479

The jail superintendent is required to move the court once an undertrial completes the period under Section 479 BNSS, and courts have directed jails to identify such prisoners. Families need not wait for this — an application can be filed directly through an advocate.

title.raw: Police Custody & Remand Hearings in Pune
title.rendered: Police Custody & Remand Hearings in Pune

content.raw:
In short

An arrested person must be produced before the nearest Magistrate within 24 hours, excluding travel time (Section 58 BNSS). At that hearing the police may ask for police custody (detention with the police for questioning) or the court may send the person to judicial custody (jail). Under Section 187 BNSS, police custody can total at most 15 days, taken in one stretch or in parts during the first 40 or 60 days. The remand hearing is the first chance for a defence advocate to be heard.

What the family should do in the first hours

  1. Find out the police station and the FIR number (or the sections applied). The police must inform a relative or friend of the arrest (Section 48 BNSS).
  2. Ask for the grounds of arrest. The arrested person is entitled to know them, and to know whether the offence is bailable (Section 47 BNSS).
  3. Contact an advocate before the production, so the remand application can be opposed and, where available, bail can be moved the same day.
  4. Collect documents: identity proof, address proof, and anything showing roots in Pune (employment, family, property).
  5. Do not discuss the facts with the police or others on the person’s behalf.

Police custody vs judicial custody

Police custodyJudicial custody
WherePolice lock-upJail (e.g. Yerawada)
PurposeInvestigation — questioning, recoveryDetention while investigation continues
Limit15 days in total (S.187)Up to 60 / 90 days before charge-sheet
BailA bail application can be filed in either case

How a remand hearing is opposed

  • Whether the arrest itself complied with the law — grounds of arrest, information to relatives, the notice procedure for offences punishable up to seven years (Section 35 BNSS).
  • Whether the police have shown specific reasons for custodial questioning, or only repeated general grounds.
  • Whether recoveries are already complete, making further police custody unnecessary.
  • Medical examination of the arrested person where there is any complaint of ill-treatment.

After remand: the 60/90-day rule

If the police do not file the charge-sheet within 60 days (or 90 days for offences punishable with death, life imprisonment or ten years or more), the accused has a right to default bail — provided the application is made before the charge-sheet is filed.

Related

  • Your rights when arrested
  • A family member was arrested last night — read this first
  • Bail applications

How many days of remand can the police get?

Under Section 187 BNSS (old Section 167 CrPC), police custody can total at most 15 days. Unlike the old law, these 15 days can be taken in one stretch or in parts at any time during the first 40 days of detention (for offences punishable up to ten years) or the first 60 days (for more serious offences). Every remand must be ordered by a Magistrate, who must be satisfied that further detention is necessary.

Can a remand order be challenged?

Yes. A remand order can be challenged in revision before the Sessions Court. Where the arrest or detention itself is illegal — for example, the arrested person was not produced within 24 hours, or the grounds of arrest were not supplied — a habeas corpus petition before the High Court may lie. The Supreme Court has held that the grounds of arrest must be communicated to the arrested person in writing.

पोलीस कोठडी / न्यायालयीन कोठडी (Marathi & Hindi)

पोलीस कोठडी म्हणजे तपासासाठी आरोपीला पोलिसांकडे ठेवणे — एकूण जास्तीत जास्त १५ दिवस. न्यायालयीन कोठडी म्हणजे आरोपीला जेलमध्ये (उदा. येरवडा) ठेवणे. दोन्ही वेळी जामीन अर्ज करता येतो. जामीन — मराठी माहिती.

पुलिस रिमांड का मतलब है जांच के लिए आरोपी को पुलिस हिरासत में रखना — कुल अधिकतम 15 दिन। न्यायिक हिरासत का मतलब है जेल में रखना। दोनों में जमानत अर्जी दी जा सकती है।

Visiting a person in Yerawada jail (judicial custody)

Family members can meet a prisoner in judicial custody under the jail’s visit (mulakat) rules; Maharashtra prisons also allow visits to be booked online through the e-Mulakat / ePrisons system. Clothing, money and medicines are accepted only as the jail rules permit, so check the current procedure with the jail before visiting. The advocate can meet the accused separately for the case.

title.raw: Sessions Trial Defence Lawyer in Pune
title.rendered: Sessions Trial Defence Lawyer in Pune

content.raw:
In short

Offences such as murder, attempt to murder, rape, POCSO, NDPS commercial-quantity and dacoity are tried by the Sessions Court. After the charge-sheet, the case is committed by the Magistrate (Section 232 BNSS), the defence may seek discharge (Section 250), the court frames charges (Section 251), the prosecution leads evidence, the defence cross-examines every witness, the accused is examined on the evidence (Section 351), and the court hears final arguments before judgment.

Stages of a Sessions trial

StageBNSSWhat the defence does
CommittalS.232Checks that all documents relied on by the prosecution have been supplied.
DischargeS.250Argues that the material, taken at face value, does not disclose the offence. Must ordinarily be filed within 60 days of committal.
Framing of chargeS.251Opposes charges not supported by the record — a wrong charge shapes the whole trial.
Prosecution evidenceS.254Cross-examines each witness — the stage where most trials are won or lost.
No-evidence acquittalS.255Seeks acquittal if there is no evidence that the accused committed the offence.
Statement of accusedS.351Prepares the accused to explain circumstances put to them.
Defence evidence & argumentsS.256–257Leads defence witnesses where useful; written and oral arguments on the record.

Where trials are actually decided

  • Cross-examination. Contradictions between a witness’s police statement and court testimony, gaps in the panchnama, chain of custody of seized articles, and the timing of the FIR.
  • Medical and forensic evidence. Whether injuries match the alleged weapon; whether forensic reports were properly sent and received.
  • Electronic evidence. Certificates and the integrity of call records, CCTV and phone data.
  • Procedure. Arrest, search and seizure rules — strict in NDPS and POCSO matters.

Bail during trial

Bail can be sought at any stage, including after charges are framed. Long custody with a trial that is not progressing is a recognised ground; see default bail and undertrial release and bail applications.

Changing your lawyer during a trial

An accused may change advocates at any stage. The new advocate files a vakalatnama, obtains the record and depositions already taken, and continues from the current stage. Witnesses already examined cannot ordinarily be recalled, except under the court’s power to recall a witness where essential.

Related

  • Discharge applications
  • From FIR to verdict — the trial process explained
  • Appeals after conviction

Which cases go to the Sessions Court in Pune?

Offences triable by a Court of Session — such as murder, attempt to murder, rape, dacoity and commercial-quantity NDPS offences — are heard at the Pune District & Sessions Court, Shivajinagar. Special courts under the POCSO Act, NDPS Act, MCOCA and the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act also sit in the same complex. Matters from Pimpri-Chinchwad police stations are first heard by the Pimpri-Chinchwad court; the court to which a sessions-triable case is committed should be confirmed for each case.

Chargesheet: when it is filed and how to get a copy

The police file the chargesheet (final report) when investigation is complete — for an accused in custody, ordinarily within 60 or 90 days, failing which default bail becomes available. Once the court takes cognizance, the accused is entitled to copies of the police report and the documents relied on (Section 230 BNSS, old Section 207 CrPC). A chargesheet is not challenged by a general “objection”; the remedies are a discharge application or, in suitable cases, quashing before the High Court.

Handing over the file when you change lawyers

It is customary to obtain a no-objection from the earlier advocate before the new advocate files a vakalatnama; if that is not forthcoming, the court can permit the change. The new advocate collects the case papers and certified copies of depositions already recorded, so that the trial continues without loss of time.

In short: A person convicted in a criminal case can appeal under Section 415 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), old Section 374 CrPC. A conviction by a Sessions Judge is appealed to the Bombay High Court in Mumbai. A conviction by a Magistrate is appealed to the Sessions Court. The appeal period is 60 days for the High Court and 30 days for the Sessions Court. While the appeal is pending, the court can suspend the sentence and grant bail under Section 430 BNSS (old Section 389 CrPC).

Appeal under CrPC or BNSS: which section applies

The CrPC was replaced by the BNSS on 1 July 2024. An offence committed before that date is still tried under the old laws. For the appeal itself, one High Court has held that an appeal filed on or after 1 July 2024 follows the BNSS procedure, even if the trial was under the CrPC. Pending matters stay under the CrPC. Courts may differ, so we cite both numbers.

SubjectOld (CrPC, 1973)New (BNSS, 2023)
Appeal from convictionSection 374Section 415
No appeal on a guilty plea; petty casesSections 375, 376Sections 416, 417
Victim's right of appeal (proviso)Section 372Section 413
Appeal against acquittalSection 378Section 419
Appeal to Supreme Court after High Court reverses acquittalSection 379Section 420
Suspension of sentence / bail pending appealSection 389Section 430
Bail bond after acquittal appeal is notifiedSection 437ASection 481
RevisionSections 397 to 401Sections 438 to 442
High Court's inherent powers (quashing)Section 482Section 528

Appeal against conviction: Sessions Court or High Court

Section 415 BNSS decides the forum by who convicted:

  • Conviction by a Sessions Judge or Additional Sessions Judge: appeal to the Bombay High Court. The same applies to a conviction by any other court where a sentence of more than seven years was passed on the appellant or a co-accused.
  • Conviction by a Magistrate: appeal to the Sessions Court. For Pune and Pimpri-Chinchwad cases, this is the Pune District and Sessions Court at Shivajinagar.

The Bombay High Court sits in Mumbai. There is no Pune bench, so a High Court appeal from a Pune Sessions Court is filed in Mumbai. For Mumbai readers, matters before the Bombay High Court and Mumbai courts are handled, with consultation by phone or video. The office is in Shivajinagar, Pune.

No appeal lies in some situations, such as where the accused pleaded guilty (Section 416 BNSS) or in petty cases (Section 417). A revision may still be possible; see below.

Criminal appeal limitation: how many days

The periods come from the Limitation Act, 1963, and the BNSS sections themselves. The clock starts on the date of the sentence or order.

RemedyTime
Appeal against conviction to the High Court60 days
Appeal against conviction to the Sessions Court30 days
State appeal against acquittal90 days
Complainant's application for special leave against acquittal (Section 419 BNSS)60 days (six months if the complainant is a public servant)
Criminal revision90 days
Special leave petition in the Supreme Court90 days (60 days where the High Court refused leave to appeal or a death sentence is involved)

A court can condone delay only for sufficient cause, and it is never safe to rely on that. Time spent getting the certified copy of the judgment is generally allowed, but obtain it at once. If you are in jail, a petition can be sent through the jail authorities (Section 424 BNSS, old Section 383 CrPC).

Bail pending appeal: suspension of sentence under Section 430 BNSS

Suspension of sentence means the appellate court stops the sentence from running and releases the appellant on bail until the appeal is decided. The conviction remains. After conviction the presumption of innocence no longer works as it does before trial, so courts look at different things from a normal bail application.

  • The court must record reasons in writing (Section 430(1)).
  • Where the offence is punishable with death, life imprisonment or ten years or more, the Public Prosecutor must first be given a chance to oppose in writing.
  • If the sentence is three years or less and the person was on bail during trial, the convicting court itself must ordinarily grant bail for long enough to file the appeal, unless it records special reasons (Section 430(3)).
  • The High Court has the same power for appeals from courts below it (Section 430(2)).

Courts commonly look at the length of the sentence and time already served, whether the appeal raises arguable points, conduct on bail during trial, and whether the appeal can be heard before the sentence is served. The Supreme Court's approach differs by sentence. In Aasif @ Pasha (2025 INSC 944), it recalled that for fixed-term sentences, suspension should ordinarily be considered unless exceptional circumstances exist, and set aside a High Court refusal. In Rajesh Upadhyay (2025 INSC 1468), it held that for murder convictions with life sentences, suspension is limited to exceptional cases, and the appellate court should not re-examine the evidence at that stage.

The application is usually filed with the appeal and listed on notice to the State. For general bail law, see bail applications.

How a High Court appeal moves

  1. Certified copies of the judgment, order on sentence and trial record are obtained.
  2. Grounds of appeal are drafted from the evidence actually recorded.
  3. The appeal and the suspension application are filed together in the Bombay High Court, Mumbai.
  4. The suspension application is argued first. Admission of the appeal follows, and final hearing comes later on the full record.
  5. If the sentence is suspended, release is on bail with conditions.

A revision is not a second appeal. The High Court or the Sessions Judge can call for the record of a lower court to check that a finding, sentence or order is correct, legal and proper. It is used for legal errors, not to re-weigh evidence.

  • It cannot be used against interlocutory orders (Section 438(2)).
  • A person who applies to the Sessions Judge cannot then apply to the High Court on the same matter, and the reverse (Section 438(3)).
  • Generally, a revision cannot turn an acquittal into a conviction, and it is not available where an appeal lies and was not filed.
  • Time: 90 days from the order.

Orders on discharge or charge are often challenged this way. See discharge application and sessions trial defence.

  • State. For a Magistrate's acquittal in a cognizable, non-bailable offence, the District Magistrate may direct the Public Prosecutor to appeal to the Sessions Court.   • Complainant. In a complaint case, the complainant may apply to the High Court for special leave to appeal (Section 419(4) BNSS).
  • Victim. The proviso to Section 413 BNSS gives a victim a right to appeal against an acquittal, a conviction for a lesser offence, or inadequate compensation. After an appeal is notified, the court may require a bail bond for appearance (Section 481 BNSS).

A High Court judgment can be taken to the Supreme Court by a special leave petition (SLP) under Article 136 of the Constitution. Where the High Court reverses an acquittal and sentences a person to death, life imprisonment or ten years or more, the Supreme Court appeal is a statutory right (Section 420 BNSS, old Section 379 CrPC). The SLP period is 90 days in most cases.

  • Judgment and order on sentence
  • Charge-sheet and, if available, the witnesses' depositions and exhibits
  • Custody details: date of arrest, periods on bail, date of conviction
  • Earlier bail orders and the date the certified copy was applied for

  • Missing the 30, 60 or 90-day limit while waiting for the certified copy.
  • Filing a revision where an appeal lies, or the reverse.
  • Filing a revision in the Sessions Court and again in the High Court.
  • Asking for suspension without custody details and the points that make the appeal arguable.
  • Ignoring a State appeal against an acquittal, or a victim's appeal.

Discharge Application in a Criminal Case in Pune

Not every criminal case that reaches the charge stage deserves to go to trial. Where the material collected by the investigating agency does not, even on its face, make out a case against the accused, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), which replaced the CrPC from 1 July 2024, allows the accused to apply for discharge before charges are even framed. Discharge in Sessions cases is governed by Section 250 BNSS (formerly Section 227 CrPC), in warrant cases instituted on a police report by Section 262 BNSS (formerly Section 239 CrPC), and in cases instituted on a private complaint by Section 272 BNSS (formerly Section 245 CrPC). A successful discharge application ends the case at that stage, without the accused having to go through a full trial. We prepare and argue discharge applications for clients in Pune.

What a Discharge Application Actually Involves

  • Reviewing the chargesheet and case material — the police report, statements recorded, seized documents, and any other material the prosecution relies on, to identify gaps or contradictions that go to the root of the case.
  • Identifying legal defects — situations where the alleged facts, even if fully accepted as true, don't actually make out the ingredients of the offence charged, or where the case is barred by law (limitation, sanction requirements, or double jeopardy, for instance).
  • Drafting the application — a focused legal argument, supported by the record, on why the material does not disclose a prima facie case against the accused.
  • Arguing the application — before the trial court, at the stage before charges are framed.
  • Following through — either securing discharge and closure of the case, or, if the application is rejected, preparing for the charge-framing stage and, where appropriate, challenging the rejection before a higher court.

Who Needs This

  • Anyone who has been chargesheeted in a criminal case in Pune and believes the evidence against them does not actually support the charge.
  • Anyone named in an FIR based on a private complaint where the underlying facts, even taken at face value, do not disclose an offence.
  • Anyone facing a case where a legal bar applies — such as lack of required sanction, limitation, or the matter having already been dealt with elsewhere.
  • Anyone who wants to avoid a lengthy trial where the case against them is genuinely weak on the existing record, rather than waiting until trial to be acquitted.
  • Co-accused in a multi-person case whose individual role, on the record, does not support their continued prosecution even if the case proceeds against others.

Where These Matters Are Handled

Discharge applications are filed and argued before the same trial court where the case is pending — the JMFC court or the Sessions Court, Pune, depending on the nature and gravity of the offence. Under Section 262 BNSS, an application for discharge in a warrant case instituted on a police report must be filed within sixty days from the date the accused was supplied copies of the police report and other documents; Section 250 BNSS prescribes the same sixty-day limit, from the date of committal, in Sessions cases. If the trial court rejects the discharge application, that order can be challenged before the Sessions Court or the Bombay High Court (Principal Seat, Mumbai), depending on which court passed the original order.

What the Court Actually Weighs

At the discharge stage, the court does not weigh evidence the way it would at trial, and does not decide guilt or innocence. The test is whether, taking the material on record at face value, there is sufficient ground to presume that the accused has committed the offence — if the material, even if wholly believed, would not establish the offence, or if it is so weak, contradictory, or inherently improbable that no reasonable prosecution could be founded on it, discharge is warranted. The court also examines any legal bar to prosecution, such as absence of required government sanction, limitation issues, or a fundamental defect in how the case has been framed.

The Process

  1. Case assessment — a detailed review of the chargesheet, statements, and documents to identify whether a genuine discharge ground exists.
  2. Drafting the application — building the legal argument around the specific gaps, contradictions, or legal bars identified, supported by references to the case record.
  3. Filing — filing the application within the statutory time limit (sixty days from the relevant triggering date under the BNSS, where applicable).
  4. Hearing — arguing the application before the trial court, addressing the prosecution's response.
  5. Order — the court either discharges the accused (ending the case at that stage) or proceeds to frame charges.
  6. Next steps — where discharge is granted, ensuring the order is properly recorded and the case formally closed; where it is rejected, preparing for trial or challenging the rejection before a higher court.

POSH Act Compliance & Workplace Law in Pune

Every workplace in India with ten or more employees is legally required to prevent, prohibit, and redress sexual harassment of women, under the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 (POSH Act) — a standalone statute that was not affected by the 2023–2024 criminal law reforms. The Act requires employers to constitute an Internal Committee, adopt a written policy, and handle complaints within defined timelines, while also giving employees a clear legal route to raise a complaint and seek redress. We advise employers on setting up compliant internal processes, and represent both complainants and respondents in POSH-related proceedings in Pune.

What POSH Compliance and Representation Actually Involves

  • For employers — constituting an Internal Committee (IC) under Section 4 of the Act, drafting a POSH policy, training the IC, and setting up the annual reporting and display obligations the law requires.
  • For a complainant — assistance in drafting and submitting a written complaint to the IC under Section 9, understanding the inquiry process, and pursuing further legal remedies if the internal process is inadequate.
  • For a respondent — representation and advice through an internal inquiry, since a POSH inquiry can lead to serious service consequences including termination, and the process must still follow natural justice.
  • Appeals and civil/criminal follow-through — where the internal process does not resolve the matter, or where the underlying conduct also amounts to a criminal offence, advising on the appropriate next legal steps.

Who Needs This

  • Business owners, HR heads, and startups in Pune who need to set up a legally compliant Internal Committee and policy, or who have never formalised one.
  • An employee who has faced workplace sexual harassment and wants to file a complaint, or is unsure how the internal process works.
  • An employee or manager who has been named as a respondent in an internal complaint and needs representation through the inquiry.
  • Organisations facing scrutiny or a show-cause notice for not having a functioning Internal Committee.
  • Anyone dissatisfied with how an internal inquiry was conducted and considering further legal action.

Where These Matters Are Handled

The POSH process itself begins internally, before the workplace's own Internal Committee (or the Local Committee, for smaller establishments without ten employees, constituted at the district level). If the internal process fails to deliver a fair or timely outcome, or if the underlying facts also disclose a criminal offence, the matter can move to the Magistrate's court or, for civil consequences such as wrongful termination following a flawed inquiry, before the appropriate civil or labour forum. Serious workplace incidents that also constitute criminal offences are pursued separately before the police and the criminal courts in Pune, alongside — not instead of — the POSH process.

What the Inquiry Actually Weighs

An Internal Committee inquiry is required to follow the principles of natural justice — both sides must be heard, evidence must be properly recorded, and the process must be conducted with confidentiality. The Committee examines the conduct alleged against the definition of sexual harassment under the Act, the credibility and consistency of the accounts and any supporting evidence, and reaches a finding that supports a recommendation to the employer on the appropriate action. Employers who fail to constitute an IC, or fail to act on its findings, can themselves face penalties, including a fine of up to ₹50,000 under Section 26 and cancellation of business licences on repeat default.

The Process

  1. Case assessment — understanding whether you need compliance setup (as an employer) or representation (as a complainant or respondent), and the specific facts involved.
  2. Documentation — drafting the POSH policy and IC constitution documents for employers, or the written complaint and supporting evidence for a complainant, or the response and evidence for a respondent.
  3. Filing / submission — submitting the complaint to the Internal Committee (within three months of the incident, extendable in genuine cases) or completing the compliance documentation with the organisation.
  4. Inquiry participation — representation and preparation for hearings before the Internal Committee, including statements, cross-examination of the other side's account where permitted, and written submissions.
  5. Outcome — the Committee's report and recommendation to the employer, typically within 90 days of the complaint.
  6. Further recourse — advice on appeal options, civil remedies, or parallel criminal proceedings if the outcome is unsatisfactory or the underlying conduct warrants it.

Intellectual Property Lawyer in Pune

Trademark infringement, copyright piracy, and counterfeit goods cause real, ongoing damage to a business's brand and revenue, and Indian law gives rights holders both civil and criminal tools to stop it. Trademark owners can sue for infringement and passing off under Sections 134 and 135 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, which allow a court to grant an injunction, damages or an account of profits, and delivery-up of infringing goods. Copyright owners have parallel civil remedies under the Copyright Act, 1957 — injunction, damages, and rendition of accounts — and, where the infringement is deliberate, a criminal complaint is also available. We advise and represent individuals, professionals, and small businesses in Pune on protecting, enforcing, and defending intellectual property rights.

What IP Enforcement Actually Involves

Depending on the right involved and how it has been violated, the available remedies differ:

  • Trademark infringement / passing off — a civil suit for injunction and damages under the Trade Marks Act, 1999, and, where a mark has been deliberately falsified or falsely applied, a criminal complaint under Sections 103 to 105 of the same Act.
  • Copyright infringement — a civil suit for injunction and damages, or a criminal complaint under Section 63 of the Copyright Act, 1957 (knowing infringement), with police empowered under Section 64 to seize infringing copies without a warrant.
  • Counterfeit goods and piracy — combined civil and criminal action, often including a police complaint alongside a civil suit for an injunction.
  • Cease-and-desist and pre-litigation strategy — many disputes are resolved, or at least clarified, through a properly drafted legal notice before any suit is filed.

Who Needs This

This practice area is relevant if you are:

  • A business or professional whose trademark, logo, product packaging, or brand name is being copied or imitated.
  • A creator, publisher, or business whose copyrighted content, software, designs, or written material has been reproduced without permission.
  • A trader dealing in counterfeit or spurious goods bearing someone else's mark, and facing a criminal complaint or raid as a result.
  • A business owner who has received a cease-and-desist notice or legal proceedings alleging that you are infringing someone else's IP, and needs a defence.
  • A business that wants IP protection built into its contracts, licensing arrangements, or vendor agreements before a dispute arises.

Where These Matters Are Handled

Civil suits for trademark and copyright infringement are ordinarily filed in the District Court within whose jurisdiction the plaintiff resides, carries on business, or works for gain — for a Pune-based rights holder, this is the Pune District Court. Under the Commercial Courts Act, 2015, IP disputes that qualify as "commercial disputes" of the specified pecuniary value are heard by the Commercial Court at the District Court level; higher-value disputes go to the Commercial Division of the Bombay High Court. Criminal complaints relating to counterfeiting or copyright piracy are filed with the local police or the Magistrate's court having jurisdiction over the infringing act. Appeals from adverse orders go up to the Bombay High Court (Principal Seat, Mumbai), which since 2021 has taken over the appellate and rectification jurisdiction previously exercised by the now-abolished Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

What the Court Actually Weighs

In an infringement or passing-off suit, the court examines whether the marks or works are deceptively similar, whether the plaintiff has a prior, provable right in the mark or work, whether there is a genuine likelihood of confusion or actual copying, and — for interim relief — whether the plaintiff will suffer irreparable harm if an injunction is not granted immediately. In criminal matters, the prosecution must show that the infringement was knowing and deliberate, since good-faith or accidental similarity does not attract criminal liability in the same way.

The Process

  1. Case assessment — reviewing your registration status (or lack of it), the nature of the infringement, available evidence, and whether civil, criminal, or both routes are appropriate.
  2. Documentation and evidence gathering — collecting proof of prior use or ownership, samples of the infringing goods or content, and, where useful, a cease-and-desist notice to the other side.
  3. Filing — drafting and filing the civil suit (with an application for interim injunction where urgency demands it) or the criminal complaint, at the appropriate court.
  4. Interim relief hearing — arguing for an ad-interim or interim injunction to stop ongoing infringement while the main case proceeds.
  5. Trial / final hearing — leading evidence, cross-examination, and final arguments on the merits.
  6. Outcome and enforcement — securing the final order (permanent injunction, damages, or acquittal/conviction as applicable) and, where needed, pursuing execution or appeal.

EOW & Financial Crimes Defence in Pune

The Economic Offences Wing (EOW) is the specialised police unit that investigates cheating, criminal breach of trust, forgery, Ponzi and chit-fund fraud, and other financial crimes — offences now defined under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), which replaced the Indian Penal Code from 1 July 2024. Cheating is dealt with under Section 318 BNS (formerly Section 420 IPC), criminal breach of trust under Section 316 BNS (formerly Section 406–409 IPC), and forgery under Sections 336 to 338 BNS. In Maharashtra, deposit and investment fraud cases are frequently also booked under the state's own Maharashtra Protection of Interest of Depositors (in Financial Establishments) Act, 1999 (MPID Act), which allows attachment of the accused's assets. We represent both complainants seeking to recover money and the accused defending EOW investigations and prosecutions in Pune.

What EOW Defence and Representation Actually Involves

  • Pre-FIR intervention — where a complaint or preliminary inquiry is underway, advising on how to respond and, where appropriate, seeking to prevent registration of a case that does not disclose an offence.
  • Anticipatory and regular bail — economic offences frequently carry a real risk of arrest, and EOW/financial crime bail applications often turn on the amount involved, the number of complainants, and flight or tampering risk.
  • Defending searches, seizures, and asset attachment — particularly under the MPID Act, where the accused's properties can be attached even before conviction.
  • Chargesheet and trial defence — challenging the evidence on cheating, criminal breach of trust, or forgery, and where appropriate, seeking discharge before trial.
  • Representing complainants/victims — assisting individuals who have been defrauded in filing a complaint with the EOW or local police and pursuing recovery.

Who Needs This

  • Anyone who has received an EOW notice, summons, or has learned that a complaint has been filed against them alleging cheating, breach of trust, or forgery.
  • Business owners, directors, or partners facing allegations connected to an investment scheme, chit fund, NBFC, or deposit-taking activity that has gone bad.
  • Individuals whose bank accounts or property have been frozen or attached in connection with a financial crime investigation.
  • Investors or depositors who have lost money in a fraudulent scheme and want to file a complaint or join proceedings to recover funds.
  • Anyone under investigation in a multi-accused financial fraud case who needs independent representation distinct from co-accused.

Where These Matters Are Handled

EOW investigations in and around Pune are conducted by the Pune Police's Economic Offences Wing, with cases then proceeding before the Magistrate's court (JMFC) or the Sessions Court, Pune, depending on the offence and its punishment. MPID Act cases, given their state-wide asset-attachment framework, are tried before the Special Court designated under that Act. Bail applications that are rejected at the trial court level, and matters involving complex or high-value fraud, are taken up before the Bombay High Court (Principal Seat, Mumbai).

What the Court Actually Weighs

In economic offence bail applications, courts have repeatedly held that financial crimes involving large sums, multiple victims, or systemic fraud are treated differently from ordinary offences, given the scale of harm and the risk of evidence tampering or fleeing. The court examines the amount and number of persons affected, whether the accused's role is that of a mastermind or a peripheral participant, custodial cooperation during investigation, and the accused's willingness to cooperate with recovery or repayment where relevant. At the chargesheet stage, the court looks at whether the ingredients of cheating (dishonest inducement) or criminal breach of trust (entrustment followed by dishonest misappropriation) are actually made out on the material collected, since these are distinct offences with distinct elements that are often conflated in complaints.

The Process

  1. Case assessment — reviewing the complaint, FIR, or notice, and the underlying transaction or business dealing to understand exposure and options.
  2. Immediate protective steps — where arrest is a real risk, moving for anticipatory bail; where assets have been or may be attached, addressing that separately.
  3. Responding to investigation — cooperating with EOW summons and questioning while protecting the client's legal position, and challenging any procedural overreach.
  4. Chargesheet review — scrutinising the evidence once the chargesheet is filed, and where the ingredients of the offence are not made out, filing for discharge.
  5. Trial — defending the matter through framing of charge, evidence, and final arguments if it proceeds to trial.
  6. Outcome and follow-through — pursuing acquittal, appeal, or, where appropriate, negotiated resolution and asset release.

Corporate Legal Advisory in Pune

Small and mid-sized businesses in Pune need ongoing legal support that goes beyond dispute resolution — contracts that actually protect them, compliance that keeps them out of trouble, and sound advice before a decision is made rather than after it causes a problem. This advisory work draws on the Indian Contract Act, 1872 for agreement drafting and enforceability, the Companies Act, 2013 for corporate structuring and compliance, and the relevant state and central licensing statutes depending on the nature of the business. We advise proprietorships, partnerships, and companies in Pune on the legal side of running and protecting a business.

What Corporate Legal Advisory Actually Involves

  • Contract drafting and review — vendor agreements, service agreements, employment contracts, non-disclosure agreements, and partnership or shareholder agreements, drafted to hold up if disputed.
  • Business structuring advice — helping founders choose and set up the right structure (proprietorship, partnership, LLP, or private limited company) for their situation, and advising on the compliance obligations that come with each.
  • Regulatory and licensing compliance — Shops & Establishments registration, labour law compliance, and other sector-specific licensing that applies to the business.
  • Recovery of dues — legal notices and, where necessary, civil suits or summary proceedings to recover money owed to the business by clients, customers, or vendors.
  • Dispute avoidance and resolution — advising before a dispute escalates, and representing the business if it does end up in litigation or arbitration.

Who Needs This

  • Founders and small business owners in Pune who are entering into contracts without proper legal review, or relying on templates that don't reflect their actual business.
  • Businesses that have outgrown informal arrangements with partners, vendors, or employees and need those relationships formalised in writing.
  • Companies and LLPs that need routine compliance support — registrations, statutory filings coordination, and policy documentation.
  • Business owners facing a payment dispute, breach of contract, or a partner/vendor relationship that has broken down.
  • Anyone starting a new venture who wants the legal groundwork — structure, contracts, compliance — done properly from day one rather than fixed after a problem arises.

Most corporate advisory work — contract drafting, structuring advice, and compliance — happens outside court, as part of ongoing legal support to the business.   5. Dispute handling (if needed) — sending legal notices, pursuing recovery, or defending the business if a dispute does escalate to litigation or arbitration.
  6. Resolution — negotiated settlement, arbitral award, or court judgment, followed by enforcement where necessary.

In short: A cheque bounce case in Pune is a criminal complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (NI Act). The payee must send a legal notice within 30 days of the bank's return memo. The drawer then has 15 days to pay. If nothing is paid, the complaint must be filed within one month. The punishment is up to 2 years in prison, a fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both, and many cases end in settlement.

Cheque bounce meaning: when a returned cheque becomes a crime

A cheque "bounces" when the bank returns it unpaid. That alone is not a crime. Section 138 applies only when all of these are true:

  • The cheque was given to pay a legally enforceable debt or liability.
  • The bank returned it for insufficient funds, or because the amount exceeded the arrangement with the bank.
  • The cheque was presented within six months of its date or its validity period, whichever is earlier. Since 1 April 2012 the RBI has fixed cheque validity at three months, so in practice this means three months.
  • The payee sent a written demand notice in time, and the drawer did not pay within 15 days of receiving it.

A return for "signature differs", "account closed" or "payment stopped" raises its own legal questions. The reason on the return memo matters, so show the memo to an advocate. This page covers both the drawer (who signed the cheque) and the payee.

Cheque bounce charges: bank charges and court penalties

People searching "cheque bounce charges" usually mean one of two things.

Bank charges. Banks charge a fee when a cheque is returned. The amount is not fixed by law. Each bank sets it in its own schedule of charges, and it differs between banks and account types. Check your bank's current schedule for the exact amount.

Court penalties. These are the punishment under Section 138, explained below. A court decides them, separately from any bank charge.

Cheque bounce time limit: the deadlines under Section 138

The time limits are strict. A late notice or a late complaint can end a case, whatever the merits.

StepTime allowedCounted from
Present the cheque to the bankWithin 3 months (validity period)Date written on the cheque
Send the legal noticeWithin 30 daysThe payee receives information from the bank that the cheque is returned unpaid
Drawer pays15 daysReceipt of the notice
File the complaintWithin one monthThe day the 15-day period ends without payment (Section 142(1)(b))

The court may take up a late complaint if the complainant shows sufficient cause. This is discretionary, so do not rely on it. Count days conservatively and file before the last day.

Cheque bounce legal notice: what the payee must send

The notice should identify the cheque (number, date, amount, bank), state the date and reason of the bank's return memo, and demand payment within 15 days of receipt. Send it to the drawer's correct address by a mode that gives proof, such as speed post or registered post, and keep the tracking record.

If the drawer pays within the 15 days, no offence under Section 138 is made out. A drawer who disputes the debt should send a written reply in the same period, because the reply is often read again at trial.

Cheque bounce jurisdiction: which court hears the case (Section 142)

Section 142(2) of the NI Act, as amended in 2015, decides the court by the bank branch, not by where the drawer lives.

  • If the cheque was given for collection through the payee's account, the court is where the payee's bank branch (the branch holding the account) is located. A cheque dropped at another branch of that bank is treated as delivered to the home branch.
  • If the cheque is presented for payment otherwise than through an account, the court is where the drawer's bank branch is located.

Before the amendment, the Supreme Court in Dashrath Rupsingh Rathod v. State of Maharashtra (2014) had tied the case to the drawee bank's location. Parliament amended the law, and Section 142A moved pending complaints to the correct court. In Jai Balaji Industries Ltd. v. HEG Ltd. (2025 INSC 1362), the Supreme Court held that for an account payee cheque the payee's home branch decides the court.

So a payee whose account is at a Pune branch files before a Magistrate court in Pune, and one with a Pimpri-Chinchwad branch files in the court covering that area. For Mumbai readers: if the payee's branch is in Mumbai, a Mumbai Magistrate court hears the case. Matters before Mumbai courts and the Bombay High Court are handled, with consultation by phone or video; the office is in Shivajinagar, Pune.

Cheque bounce case procedure: what happens after the complaint

  1. Complaint. The payee files it with the cheque, return memo, notice, proof of delivery and an affidavit.
  2. Summons. The court takes cognizance and summons the accused.
  3. Appearance and bail. The accused appears and ordinarily furnishes a bail bond. Do not skip dates: repeated absence can lead to a warrant (see non-bailable warrant cancellation).
  4. Plea. The accused pleads guilty or says the case will be contested. Interim compensation can be ordered at this stage.
  5. Evidence. The complainant's evidence is usually by affidavit, followed by cross-examination.
  6. Accused's statement (Section 351 BNSS, old Section 313 CrPC), then defence evidence if any.
  7. Arguments and judgment.

Under Section 143 these cases are tried summarily, and the Magistrate can sentence up to one year in a summary trial. If a longer sentence may be needed, the Magistrate follows the regular procedure. The law asks the court to try to finish within six months of the complaint. Actual time varies by court and stage.

Cheque bounce punishment and penalty under Section 138

On conviction, the court can impose imprisonment up to 2 years, a fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both. It can direct that the fine, or part of it, be paid to the complainant as compensation (Section 395 BNSS, old Section 357 CrPC).

Interim compensation (Section 143A) and appeal deposit (Section 148)

  • Section 143A, interim compensation. The trial court may order the accused to pay the complainant up to 20% of the cheque amount while the case is pending. It is payable within 60 days, extendable by up to 30 days for sufficient cause. If the accused is later acquitted, it must be repaid with interest. In Rakesh Ranjan Shrivastava (2024 INSC 205), the Supreme Court held that this power is discretionary, not mandatory.
  • Section 148, deposit in appeal. If a convicted accused appeals, the appellate court may order a deposit of at least 20% of the fine or compensation awarded, in addition to any interim compensation paid. In Jamboo Bhandari v. M.P. State Industrial Development Corporation Ltd. (2023), the Supreme Court said the deposit should ordinarily be ordered, and that not ordering it needs special reasons.

Settlement and compounding (Section 147)

Under Section 147, every offence under the NI Act can be compounded, meaning settled and closed. The accused pays the complainant, and the court closes the case. This is how many cases end.

In September 2025, in Sanjabij Tari v. Kishore S. Borcar (2025 INSC 1158), the Supreme Court revised the cost guidelines first set in Damodar S. Prabhu v. Sayed Babalal H. (2010) 5 SCC 663. Where the court imposes costs:

  • Before the accused's evidence is recorded: no costs.
  • After defence evidence, before the Magistrate's judgment: 5% of the cheque amount.
  • Before the Sessions Court or High Court, in revision or appeal: 7.5%.
  • Before the Supreme Court: 10%.

These are guidelines; the court keeps its discretion. Special Lok Adalats for Section 138 cases are also held at the Pune District Court.

How to escape from a cheque bounce case: lawful options only

You cannot lawfully "escape" a genuine case by avoiding summons or changing address. That leads to a warrant and weakens your position. The lawful options are:

  • Pay within the 15 days. If the debt is real, payment after the notice means no offence is made out.
  • Settle. Compounding is available at every stage, and earlier is cheaper.
  • Defend on the facts or the law. Section 139 presumes the cheque was issued for a debt, but the presumption can be rebutted (Rangappa v. Sri Mohan, (2010) 11 SCC 441). Grounds commonly examined include: no legally enforceable debt; the debt already paid; a defective, late or wrongly addressed notice; a late complaint; the wrong court; a disputed signature; and, for companies, whether a director was in charge of the business (Section 141).

If you received a notice or summons, or your cheque has bounced

Accused (drawer): note the date you received the notice, since the 15 days run from receipt. Do not ignore it. Pay if the amount is owed, or send a written reply if you dispute it. Keep the envelope and payment proofs. If summons come, appear on the date.

Complainant (payee): collect the return memo and note the date. Send the notice within 30 days, wait 15 days from delivery, then file the complaint within one month in the court where your own bank branch is located.

Documents to keep

  • The original cheque and the bank's return memo with the reason
  • The legal notice, postal receipts, tracking report and any reply
  • Proof of the debt: agreement, invoices, statements, messages
  • Identity and address proof; for a company, the authority letter
  • For the accused: the summons, the complaint copy and records of payments made

Common mistakes

  • Sending the notice after 30 days, or counting from the wrong date.
  • Filing the complaint late, or in the wrong court.
  • Presenting the cheque after its validity has ended.
  • Paying in cash without a receipt or written acknowledgement.

After the trial court: appeal and the Bombay High Court

An accused convicted by a Magistrate can appeal to the Sessions Court (Section 415(3) BNSS, old Section 374(3) CrPC) and ask for the sentence to be suspended meanwhile. See criminal appeals and suspension of sentence. For a complainant after an acquittal, the Supreme Court is examining whether the High Court's special leave is needed. A February 2026 order (Everest Automobiles) referred the question to a larger bench after doubting Celestium Financial v. A. Gnanasekaran (2025). Check the current position before filing. In limited situations the Bombay High Court can also be approached: see quashing in the Bombay High Court and Bombay High Court matters.

What affects the fee

Fees depend on your side, the stage and the court, and are agreed at the first consultation. See criminal lawyer fees in Pune and criminal defence in Pune. Old and new section numbers: CrPC to BNSS table.

Frequently asked questions

Cheque bounce hone par kya karna chahiye?

If you are the payee, collect the bank's return memo and send a legal notice within 30 days. If the drawer does not pay within 15 days, file a complaint within one month. If you are the drawer, note when you received the notice and consider paying or replying in writing within 15 days.

What is the punishment for cheque bounce under Section 138?

Up to 2 years in prison, a fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both. The court can direct that the fine be paid to the complainant as compensation.

How can I get out of a cheque bounce case legally?

Pay within the 15-day notice period, settle with the complainant at any stage, or defend the case on the facts and the law.

What are cheque bounce charges?

Bank charges for a returned cheque are set by each bank and are not fixed by law, so check your bank's schedule of charges. The court penalty for the offence is the Section 138 punishment of imprisonment, fine, or both.

What is the time limit for a cheque bounce case?

Present the cheque within its validity, send the notice within 30 days of the return information, allow 15 days to pay, and file the complaint within one month after that. A late complaint is heard only if the court accepts sufficient cause.

Can a cheque bounce case be filed in Pune if the accused lives elsewhere?

Yes, if the payee's account branch is in Pune or Pimpri-Chinchwad, an accused living elsewhere can be summoned there. Under Section 142(2), the bank branch decides the court, not the drawer's address.

Is there a new law for cheque bounce?

Section 138 itself was not changed by the BNSS in July 2024. Recent changes are the 2015 jurisdiction amendment, the 2018 additions of Sections 143A and 148, and the Supreme Court's September 2025 compounding guidelines in Sanjabij Tari.

Can a cheque bounce case be settled after the complaint is filed?

Yes. Section 147 makes the offence compoundable, so the parties can settle at any stage, including in a Lok Adalat. Costs rise at later stages.

If you need advice on your situation, you can contact the office.

This page explains the law in general terms and is not legal advice. Every case depends on its own facts.

These are guidelines; the court keeps its discretion. Special Lok Adalats for Section 138 cases are also held at the Pune District Court.

How to escape from a cheque bounce case: lawful options only

You cannot lawfully “escape” a genuine case by avoiding summons or changing address. That leads to a warrant and weakens your position. The lawful options are:

  • Pay within the 15 days. If the debt is real, payment after the notice means no offence is made out.
  • Settle. Compounding is available at every stage, and earlier is cheaper.
  • Defend on the facts or the law. Section 139 presumes the cheque was issued for a debt, but the presumption can be rebutted (Rangappa v. Sri Mohan, (2010) 11 SCC 441). Grounds commonly examined include: no legally enforceable debt; the debt already paid; a defective, late or wrongly addressed notice; a late complaint; the wrong court; a disputed signature; and, for companies, whether a director was in charge of the business (Section 141).

If you received a notice or summons, or your cheque has bounced

Accused (drawer): note the date you received the notice, since the 15 days run from receipt. Do not ignore it. Pay if the amount is owed, or send a written reply if you dispute it. Keep the envelope and payment proofs. If summons come, appear on the date.

Complainant (payee): collect the return memo and note the date. Send the notice within 30 days, wait 15 days from delivery, then file the complaint within one month in the court where your own bank branch is located.

Documents to keep

  • The original cheque and the bank’s return memo with the reason
  • The legal notice, postal receipts, tracking report and any reply
  • Proof of the debt: agreement, invoices, statements, messages
  • Identity and address proof; for a company, the authority letter
  • For the accused: the summons, the complaint copy and records of payments made

Common mistakes

  • Sending the notice after 30 days, or counting from the wrong date.
  • Filing the complaint late, or in the wrong court.
  • Presenting the cheque after its validity has ended.
  • Paying in cash without a receipt or written acknowledgement.

After the trial court: appeal and the Bombay High Court

An accused convicted by a Magistrate can appeal to the Sessions Court (Section 415(3) BNSS, old Section 374(3) CrPC) and ask for the sentence to be suspended meanwhile. See criminal appeals and suspension of sentence. For a complainant after an acquittal, the Supreme Court is examining whether the High Court’s special leave is needed. A February 2026 order (Everest Automobiles) referred the question to a larger bench after doubting Celestium Financial v. A. Gnanasekaran (2025). Check the current position before filing. In limited situations the Bombay High Court can also be approached: see quashing in the Bombay High Court and Bombay High Court matters.

What affects the fee

Fees depend on your side, the stage and the court, and are agreed at the first consultation. See criminal lawyer fees in Pune and criminal defence in Pune. Old and new section numbers: CrPC to BNSS table.

Frequently asked questions

Cheque bounce hone par kya karna chahiye?

If you are the payee, collect the bank’s return memo and send a legal notice within 30 days. If the drawer does not pay within 15 days, file a complaint within one month. If you are the drawer, note when you received the notice and consider paying or replying in writing within 15 days.

What is the punishment for cheque bounce under Section 138?

Up to 2 years in prison, a fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both. The court can direct that the fine be paid to the complainant as compensation.

How can I get out of a cheque bounce case legally?

Pay within the 15-day notice period, settle with the complainant at any stage, or defend the case on the facts and the law.

What are cheque bounce charges?

Bank charges for a returned cheque are set by each bank and are not fixed by law, so check your bank’s schedule of charges. The court penalty for the offence is the Section 138 punishment of imprisonment, fine, or both.

What is the time limit for a cheque bounce case?

Present the cheque within its validity, send the notice within 30 days of the return information, allow 15 days to pay, and file the complaint within one month after that. A late complaint is heard only if the court accepts sufficient cause.

Can a cheque bounce case be filed in Pune if the accused lives elsewhere?

Yes, if the payee’s account branch is in Pune or Pimpri-Chinchwad, an accused living elsewhere can be summoned there. Under Section 142(2), the bank branch decides the court, not the drawer’s address.

Is there a new law for cheque bounce?

Section 138 itself was not changed by the BNSS in July 2024. Recent changes are the 2015 jurisdiction amendment, the 2018 additions of Sections 143A and 148, and the Supreme Court’s September 2025 compounding guidelines in Sanjabij Tari.

Can a cheque bounce case be settled after the complaint is filed?

Yes. Section 147 makes the offence compoundable, so the parties can settle at any stage, including in a Lok Adalat. Costs rise at later stages.

The Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 is a special central statute defining specific offences against members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes under Section 3, with enhanced punishments and a distinct procedure. Cases under the Act are tried by the Special Court or Exclusive Special Court designated for the purpose under Section 14 — in Maharashtra, Sessions Courts notified for this purpose, including in Pune, function as the Special Court for SC/ST Act cases arising within their jurisdiction. MCOCA Defence Lawyer in Pune

The Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act, 1999 (MCOCA) is a stringent state law aimed at organised crime syndicates, and it is one of the most serious statutes an accused can face — it carries its own definition of "organised crime" under Section 2, its own special courts under Sections 5 to 8, and materially stricter bail conditions under Section 21 than ordinary criminal law. Where MCOCA applies alongside the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS, which replaced the CrPC from 1 July 2024), MCOCA's provisions prevail over the general law to the extent of any conflict. We defend individuals accused under MCOCA in Pune, from the investigation stage through trial and appeal.

What MCOCA Defence Actually Involves

  • Challenging invocation of MCOCA itself — MCOCA can only be invoked where the statutory preconditions are met, including prior registration of qualifying offences against the accused within the period the Act specifies, and prior sanction from a competent authority; where these preconditions are not genuinely satisfied, that is often the strongest ground of defence.
  • Bail applications — under Section 21(4), bail requires the court to be satisfied there are reasonable grounds to believe the accused is not guilty and is unlikely to commit an offence while on bail — a materially higher bar than ordinary bail, but not an absolute one.
  • Defending proclamation and absconder proceedings — where a person is declared a proclaimed offender in connection with an MCOCA case, that declaration itself can be challenged through writ proceedings before the Bombay High Court.
  • Trial defence — before the Special Court, given MCOCA's distinct evidentiary provisions, including the admissibility of certain intercepted communications and confessions made to senior police officers, both of which require careful scrutiny.
  • Appeals — against conviction, sentence, or interlocutory orders, before the Bombay High Court.

Who Needs This

  • Anyone named as an accused in an FIR or chargesheet invoking MCOCA, whether as an alleged member of an organised crime syndicate or otherwise.
  • Anyone facing arrest, in custody, or applying for bail in an MCOCA matter, given the heightened statutory bar under Section 21(4).
  • Anyone declared or facing proclamation proceedings in connection with an MCOCA case.
  • Family members of an accused trying to understand the process, the special court's procedure, and the realistic options available.
  • Anyone who believes MCOCA has been invoked against them without the statutory preconditions genuinely being satisfied.

Where These Matters Are Handled

MCOCA cases are tried before the Special Court constituted under Sections 5 to 8 of the Act, staffed by judges nominated by the state government in concurrence with the Chief Justice of the Bombay High Court. Bail applications that are rejected at the Special Court, writ petitions challenging invocation of the Act or proclamation proceedings, and appeals against conviction or sentence are taken up before the Bombay High Court (Principal Seat, Mumbai). We have represented clients in exactly this kind of proceeding — in one matter, Rupesh Marne — MCOCA + BNSS — Proclamation Stayed via Writ Petition — 2025:BHC-AS:29231, a stay was secured on proclamation proceedings through a writ petition before the Bombay High Court.

What the Court Actually Weighs

At the threshold, the court examines whether the statutory preconditions for invoking MCOCA are genuinely satisfied — the required prior registration of qualifying offences, the syndicate element, and proper sanction — since MCOCA cannot simply be layered onto an ordinary case to attract its stricter provisions. At the bail stage, the twin conditions under Section 21(4) apply cumulatively: the court must be satisfied there are reasonable grounds to believe the accused is not guilty, and that they are not likely to commit an offence while on bail. In proclamation and absconder matters, the court examines whether procedural safeguards, including proper service of process, were actually followed before such a serious step was taken.

The Process

  1. Case assessment — reviewing the FIR, chargesheet, and sanction order to examine whether MCOCA has been properly and lawfully invoked in the first place.
  2. Immediate protective steps — addressing arrest risk, custody status, or proclamation proceedings as a priority, given how serious and fast-moving these can become.
  3. Drafting and filing — the bail application, writ petition, or discharge application, built around the specific defect or defence identified in the case assessment.
  4. Hearing — representation before the Special Court or the Bombay High Court, as the matter requires.
  5. Trial defence (if the matter proceeds) — scrutiny of the prosecution's evidence, including any intercepted communications or confessional statements, through the Special Court trial.
  6. Outcome and appeal — pursuing bail, discharge, acquittal, or appeal before the Bombay High Court as the case requires.

Family Law & Divorce in Pune

A marriage breaking down is rarely just a legal event — it is a financial, parental, and personal one happening at the same time. The law gives you several distinct routes depending on whether both spouses agree to separate, whether one is contesting, whether children are involved, and whether either party needs interim financial support while the matter is pending. Each route has its own procedure, timeline, and evidentiary requirements, and choosing the wrong one, or filing it incorrectly, can add months or years to what should be a resolvable matter.

This page covers the core civil family-law remedies — divorce, custody, and maintenance — under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 and the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), as they are actually handled at the Family Court in Pune. It does not cover criminal complaints under Section 85 BNS (formerly Section 498A IPC) or the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act (PWDVA) — those are separate criminal and quasi-criminal remedies with their own procedure, addressed on this site's 498A and domestic violence defence page.

Mutual Consent Divorce — Section 13B, Hindu Marriage Act

Where both spouses agree that the marriage has broken down and are willing to separate on agreed terms, Section 13B of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 provides the fastest route to a decree. The process requires:

  • A joint petition stating the parties have lived separately for at least one year, have been unable to live together, and have mutually agreed the marriage should be dissolved
  • Agreement on ancillary matters — maintenance/alimony (if any), custody and visitation arrangements for children, and division of property or streedhan
  • Two motions before the Family Court: the first when the petition is filed, and the second after a statutory cooling-off period, confirming that consent has not been withdrawn

The six-month cooling-off period. Section 13B(2) ordinarily requires a minimum six-month gap between the first and second motions, intended to allow for reconciliation. The Supreme Court, in Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur (2017) 8 SCC 746, held that this waiting period is directory rather than mandatory, and that a Family Court has discretion to waive it where the parties have genuinely settled all disputes (alimony, custody, property), there is no possibility of reconciliation, and they have been living separately for the statutory period or longer. Waiver is not automatic — it is an application made to the court on the specific facts, and whether a given Pune Family Court bench grants it depends on how the settlement and the surrounding facts are presented. Where consent is genuinely mutual and the ancillary terms are already settled, this can meaningfully shorten a case that would otherwise run six to eighteen months.

If either party withdraws consent before the second motion, the petition fails and the matter would need to proceed as a contested divorce instead.

Contested Divorce — Section 13, Hindu Marriage Act

Where one spouse does not consent, divorce must be sought on one of the specific grounds set out in Section 13 of the Hindu Marriage Act. The commonly pleaded grounds include:

  • Cruelty — physical or mental cruelty of a degree that makes it unreasonable to expect the petitioner to continue living with the respondent
  • Desertion — continuous desertion for a period of at least two years immediately preceding the petition, without reasonable cause and without consent
  • Adultery
  • Conversion — the respondent ceasing to be a Hindu by conversion to another religion
  • Mental disorder — of a kind and degree that the petitioner cannot reasonably be expected to live with the respondent
  • Communicable disease (as specified under the Act)
  • Renunciation — the respondent having renounced the world by entering a religious order
  • Presumption of death — no news of the respondent being alive for seven years or more

A contested divorce is a full civil trial: petition, written statement, framing of issues, evidence (affidavits and cross-examination), and final arguments before judgment. This is a materially longer and more evidence-intensive process than mutual consent, and outcome depends heavily on how well the specific ground is pleaded and proved — vague allegations of "cruelty" without particulars rarely succeed. Where reconciliation genuinely is not possible, the more useful strategic move is often to test whether the other side will actually engage on a mutual consent settlement before committing to years of contested litigation.

Maintenance and Alimony

Financial support during and after divorce proceedings comes through more than one legal route, and it matters which one applies:

  • Interim maintenance under Section 144, BNSS (which replaced Section 125 of the CrPC) allows a spouse (and children, and in some cases parents) unable to maintain themselves to seek monthly maintenance from the other spouse while proceedings are pending, and this remedy is available regardless of religion. It is decided on affidavit evidence of income and needs, and can be varied later if circumstances change.
  • Permanent alimony under Section 25, Hindu Marriage Act is decided as part of, or after, the divorce decree itself, and can be awarded as a lump sum, periodic payment, or both, taking into account both parties' income, property, and conduct.
  • Maintenance amounts are fact-specific — there is no fixed formula in law — and are assessed against both spouses' actual income, earning capacity, standard of living during the marriage, and reasonable needs, including of any children.

Child Custody

Where minor children are involved, custody and visitation are decided independently of who is "at fault" in the divorce. Indian courts, including the Pune Family Court, apply the best-interest-of-the-child standard — the child's welfare, stability, and safety take priority over either parent's individual claim. Relevant factors typically include:

  • The child's age (courts generally favour the mother's custody for very young children, though this is a presumption, not an absolute rule)
  • The child's own preference, where the child is old enough to express a reasoned view
  • Each parent's ability to provide a stable home, education, and emotional environment
  • Evidence of neglect, abuse, or instability on either side

Custody orders in India are commonly structured as physical custody with one parent and defined visitation rights for the other, though joint or shared custody arrangements are increasingly recognised where practical and in the child's interest. Custody and visitation terms can also be revisited later if circumstances materially change.

How These Matters Proceed at Pune Family Court

Family law matters involving spouses ordinarily resident in Pune are filed before the Pune Family Court, established under the Family Courts Act, 1984, which has exclusive jurisdiction over matrimonial matters, maintenance, custody, and related disputes for parties within its territorial limits — distinct from the ordinary civil courts and from the Sessions Court, which handles criminal matters. Family Court proceedings are intended to be less adversarial in form: the court can require an attempt at conciliation before the matter proceeds to trial, in-camera hearings are used where appropriate, and parties are generally expected (though not always required) to appear without extensive procedural formality compared to a regular civil suit.

Realistic timelines vary widely by case type and by how contested the ancillary issues are. A well-settled mutual consent petition with the cooling-off period waived can conclude in a matter of months; a contested divorce with disputed custody and maintenance can run considerably longer, simply because of the evidentiary process a contested matter requires. No responsible advocate should quote a fixed timeline before reviewing the actual facts — settlement posture, documentary evidence, and the specific bench all affect how a case moves.
