Where both spouses agree that the marriage has broken down and are willing to separate on agreed terms, Section 13B of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 provides the fastest route to a decree. The process requires:

  • A joint petition stating the parties have lived separately for at least one year, have been unable to live together, and have mutually agreed the marriage should be dissolved
  • Agreement on ancillary matters — maintenance/alimony (if any), custody and visitation arrangements for children, and division of property or streedhan
  • Two motions before the Family Court: the first when the petition is filed, and the second after a statutory cooling-off period, confirming that consent has not been withdrawn

The six-month cooling-off period. Section 13B(2) ordinarily requires a minimum six-month gap between the first and second motions, intended to allow for reconciliation. The Supreme Court, in Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur (2017) 8 SCC 746, held that this waiting period is directory rather than mandatory, and that a Family Court has discretion to waive it where the parties have genuinely settled all disputes (alimony, custody, property), there is no possibility of reconciliation, and they have been living separately for the statutory period or longer. Waiver is not automatic — it is an application made to the court on the specific facts, and whether a given Pune Family Court bench grants it depends on how the settlement and the surrounding facts are presented. Where consent is genuinely mutual and the ancillary terms are already settled, this can meaningfully shorten a case that would otherwise run six to eighteen months.

If either party withdraws consent before the second motion, the petition fails and the matter would need to proceed as a contested divorce instead.

Contested Divorce — Section 13, Hindu Marriage Act

Where one spouse does not consent, divorce must be sought on one of the specific grounds set out in Section 13 of the Hindu Marriage Act. The commonly pleaded grounds include:

  • Cruelty — physical or mental cruelty of a degree that makes it unreasonable to expect the petitioner to continue living with the respondent
  • Desertion — continuous desertion for a period of at least two years immediately preceding the petition, without reasonable cause and without consent
  • Adultery
  • Conversion — the respondent ceasing to be a Hindu by conversion to another religion
  • Mental disorder — of a kind and degree that the petitioner cannot reasonably be expected to live with the respondent
  • Communicable disease (as specified under the Act)
  • Renunciation — the respondent having renounced the world by entering a religious order
  • Presumption of death — no news of the respondent being alive for seven years or more

A contested divorce is a full civil trial: petition, written statement, framing of issues, evidence (affidavits and cross-examination), and final arguments before judgment. This is a materially longer and more evidence-intensive process than mutual consent, and outcome depends heavily on how well the specific ground is pleaded and proved — vague allegations of "cruelty" without particulars rarely succeed. Where reconciliation genuinely is not possible, the more useful strategic move is often to test whether the other side will actually engage on a mutual consent settlement before committing to years of contested litigation.

Maintenance and Alimony

Financial support during and after divorce proceedings comes through more than one legal route, and it matters which one applies:

  • Interim maintenance under Section 144, BNSS (which replaced Section 125 of the CrPC) allows a spouse (and children, and in some cases parents) unable to maintain themselves to seek monthly maintenance from the other spouse while proceedings are pending, and this remedy is available regardless of religion. It is decided on affidavit evidence of income and needs, and can be varied later if circumstances change.
  • Permanent alimony under Section 25, Hindu Marriage Act is decided as part of, or after, the divorce decree itself, and can be awarded as a lump sum, periodic payment, or both, taking into account both parties' income, property, and conduct.
  • Maintenance amounts are fact-specific — there is no fixed formula in law — and are assessed against both spouses' actual income, earning capacity, standard of living during the marriage, and reasonable needs, including of any children.

Child Custody

Where minor children are involved, custody and visitation are decided independently of who is "at fault" in the divorce. Indian courts, including the Pune Family Court, apply the best-interest-of-the-child standard — the child's welfare, stability, and safety take priority over either parent's individual claim. Relevant factors typically include:

  • The child's age (courts generally favour the mother's custody for very young children, though this is a presumption, not an absolute rule)
  • The child's own preference, where the child is old enough to express a reasoned view
  • Each parent's ability to provide a stable home, education, and emotional environment
  • Evidence of neglect, abuse, or instability on either side

Custody orders in India are commonly structured as physical custody with one parent and defined visitation rights for the other, though joint or shared custody arrangements are increasingly recognised where practical and in the child's interest. Custody and visitation terms can also be revisited later if circumstances materially change.

How These Matters Proceed at Pune Family Court

Family law matters involving spouses ordinarily resident in Pune are filed before the Pune Family Court, established under the Family Courts Act, 1984, which has exclusive jurisdiction over matrimonial matters, maintenance, custody, and related disputes for parties within its territorial limits — distinct from the ordinary civil courts and from the Sessions Court, which handles criminal matters. Family Court proceedings are intended to be less adversarial in form: the court can require an attempt at conciliation before the matter proceeds to trial, in-camera hearings are used where appropriate, and parties are generally expected (though not always required) to appear without extensive procedural formality compared to a regular civil suit.

Realistic timelines vary widely by case type and by how contested the ancillary issues are. A well-settled mutual consent petition with the cooling-off period waived can conclude in a matter of months; a contested divorce with disputed custody and maintenance can run considerably longer, simply because of the evidentiary process a contested matter requires. No responsible advocate should quote a fixed timeline before reviewing the actual facts — settlement posture, documentary evidence, and the specific bench all affect how a case moves.

Cyber & IT Law in Pune

Cybercrime cases turn on two things most criminal lawyers never formally study: how the Information Technology Act, 2000 actually applies to a given fact pattern, and how digital material becomes admissible evidence in an Indian courtroom. Advocate Akash R. Chikate holds an LL.M in Science & Technology Laws (First Class Distinction) from Savitribai Phule Pune University and a Diploma in Cyber Laws, in addition to practicing criminal defence before the Pune Sessions Court and the Bombay High Court since 2021. That combination — a formal, examined qualification in this specific subject alongside active criminal trial practice — is uncommon in Pune's criminal defence bar, where cyber matters are usually handled as an extension of general criminal work rather than as a specialisation in their own right.

This page covers the IT Act offences that generate the bulk of cybercrime FIRs, how the 2023 evidence law recodification changed the rules for admitting electronic material, and what actually matters when building a defence once a device has been seized.

Identity Theft and Impersonation — Section 66C, IT Act

Section 66C punishes fraudulent or dishonest use of another person's electronic signature, password, or any other unique identification feature — the provision typically invoked when someone's Aadhaar details, login credentials, digital signature, or biometric identifiers are misused to impersonate them online. Conviction carries imprisonment up to three years and a fine up to ₹1 lakh. In practice, S.66C is frequently charged alongside cheating provisions under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, since the identity theft is rarely the end goal — it is the mechanism for a further fraud.

Cheating by Personation Using a Computer Resource — Section 66D, IT Act

Section 66D is the single most commonly invoked cybercrime section in Pune FIRs today, because it covers the fact pattern behind the overwhelming majority of digital fraud complaints: UPI fraud, fake customer-care calls, OTP-based bank fraud, fraudulent loan or investment apps, and impersonation on messaging platforms to extract money. The section punishes cheating by personation by means of any communication device or computer resource, with imprisonment up to three years and a fine up to ₹1 lakh. Because it is the default charging section for almost any digital fraud, S.66D FIRs range enormously in seriousness and quality of evidence — from cases with a clear, traceable money trail to cases built on a complainant's assumption of who was on the other end of a call or chat, with the actual identification evidence thin. That distinction is exactly where a defence is built or lost.

Violation of Privacy — Section 66E, IT Act

Section 66E addresses intentional capture, publication, or transmission of an image of a person's private area without their consent, in circumstances violating privacy — imprisonment up to three years or a fine up to ₹2 lakh, or both. This section is fact-specific and consent-dependent, and cases frequently turn on what was actually captured, whether consent existed and to what scope, and whether the accused was the person who transmitted or published the material versus merely possessed it.

Obscene and Sexually Explicit Content — Sections 67 and 67A, IT Act

Section 67 punishes publishing or transmitting obscene material in electronic form; Section 67A carries enhanced punishment where the material contains a sexually explicit act. These are among the more severely punished IT Act offences — S.67 carries up to three years and a fine up to ₹5 lakh on first conviction (five years and ₹10 lakh on a subsequent conviction), with S.67A carrying up to five years and a fine up to ₹10 lakh on first conviction (seven years on a subsequent one). Where a minor is involved, these sections operate alongside — not instead of — the POCSO Act, which materially changes both the forum and the stakes. Given the severity and the frequent involvement of forwarded or third-party content, the question of who actually authored, uploaded, or knowingly forwarded material — versus who merely received it — is often the entire case.

Digital Evidence Admissibility Under BSA 2023

Every cybercrime prosecution eventually reduces to a single question: is the electronic material the prosecution is relying on actually admissible? Since 1 July 2024, this is governed by Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA), which replaced Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. The core requirement is unchanged in principle — electronic records (call data, chat logs, CCTV footage, server logs, forensic images of a device) are not automatically admissible; they require a certificate confirming how the record was produced and that the device was functioning properly at the relevant time. What changed under S.63 BSA is the certificate itself: it now requires dual certification — one from the person in charge of the device or computer system, and a second, independent certification, structured in the specific Part A / Part B format set out in the BSA's Schedule. A certificate that meets the old S.65B standard but not the new dual-certification structure is a live admissibility issue, and prosecutions built on evidence gathered before the transition need careful scrutiny of which framework actually governs the certificate produced.

This is not a technicality that only matters to specialists — it is frequently the difference between a chat log or call record being read into evidence at all.

Building a Defence: Seizure, Forensics, and Chain of Custody

Once a device — a phone, laptop, or storage medium — is seized in connection with a cybercrime investigation, several practical issues routinely decide whether the resulting evidence stands up:

  • Seizure documentation. Was the seizure memo properly prepared, witnessed, and does it accurately describe what was taken, including make, model, and any identifying marks or hash values recorded at the time of seizure? Investigating officers can compel production of documents and digital data under Section 94 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (which replaced Section 91 CrPC and explicitly extends to digital material) — whether that power was exercised and documented correctly is often the first thing worth examining.
  • Chain of custody. Between seizure and forensic examination, was the device secured against tampering, and can the prosecution account for every hand it passed through? A gap or an unexplained handling event in the custody chain is one of the most reliable grounds for challenging the reliability of what a forensic report later claims to have found.
  • Forensic imaging integrity. Was a proper forensic (bit-by-bit) image taken before analysis, with hash values recorded and matched, or was the original device itself examined and potentially altered in the process?
  • Certificate compliance. Does the S.63 BSA certificate actually meet the dual-certification requirement described above, in the prescribed format, for every piece of electronic evidence the prosecution intends to rely on?
  • Attribution. Even where a message, transaction, or upload is genuine, is there actual evidence the accused — specifically — was the person who sent it, versus evidence only that it originated from a device, SIM, or account that could have been accessed by others?

None of these points, on their own, guarantee an outcome — but a defence that is built around the actual evidentiary record, rather than a general denial, is the difference between a filing that gets taken seriously and one that does not.

498A / Domestic Violence Defence in Pune

A complaint under Section 85 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) — the recodified successor to Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code — is one of the most consequential things that can happen to a family. It is also, as courts at every level including the Supreme Court have acknowledged, a provision that is sometimes invoked with vague, omnibus allegations against an entire marital family rather than specific, provable conduct by a specific person. This page is written for people on the receiving end of such a complaint: husbands, in-laws, and other relatives named as accused, who need a defence built on the actual law and actual procedure — not on minimising genuine domestic cruelty, which the law is rightly designed to punish, but on ensuring that an accusation is tested, not assumed.

What Section 85 BNS Actually Criminalizes

Section 85 BNS punishes a husband or relative of the husband who subjects a woman to cruelty, with imprisonment of up to three years and a fine. The word "cruelty" is not left undefined — Section 86 BNS (the successor to the Explanation under the old Section 498A IPC) gives it a specific, two-limb meaning:

  • Wilful conduct of a nature likely to drive the woman to suicide, or to cause grave injury or danger to her life, limb, or health — mental or physical; or
  • Harassment connected to a demand for property or valuable security — including harassment of the woman, or of anyone related to her, to coerce that demand, or as a consequence of a failure to meet it.

This matters for defence purposes because it means not every marital disagreement, every instance of friction between a wife and her in-laws, or every unhappy household qualifies. The statute requires conduct that meets one of these two specific thresholds. A significant part of building a defence is testing whether the allegations, as pleaded, actually describe conduct falling within Section 86 BNS, or whether they are general, undated, and interchangeable across every named accused — a pattern courts have repeatedly flagged as a hallmark of over-implication rather than genuine cruelty.

The offence is cognizable and non-bailable, which is precisely why the safeguards described below exist.

Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar and Why It Matters to the Accused

In Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar, (2014) 8 SCC 273, the Supreme Court addressed the routine, near-automatic arrest of husbands and their relatives the moment a Section 498A complaint (now Section 85 BNS) was registered — arrests the Court found were frequently made without any independent application of mind to whether arrest was actually necessary. The Court held that for offences punishable with imprisonment up to seven years, police officers cannot arrest mechanically merely because an FIR has been registered. They must be satisfied, under the checklist in what is now Section 35 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), that arrest is necessary to prevent further offending, ensure proper investigation, prevent tampering with evidence or influencing witnesses, or prevent the accused from absconding. Where those conditions are not independently satisfied, the police are required to issue a notice of appearance under Section 35(3) BNSS (formerly Section 41A CrPC) instead of arresting outright, and a Magistrate authorising further detention must independently record satisfaction that the arrest was justified.

Practically, this means an FIR under Section 85 BNS does not, by itself, mean the police will or should arrest. It means the accused's advocate has a specific, binding legal standard to invoke — at the police station, before the Magistrate, and in a bail application — to argue that mechanical arrest is exactly what the Supreme Court prohibited. In our experience, a large share of the anxiety in the first days after a 498A complaint comes from an assumption that arrest is inevitable. It is not, and the Arnesh Kumar safeguards are the legal reason why.

Anticipatory Bail in 498A Matters

Section 85 BNS complaints are one of the most common contexts in which anticipatory bail under Section 482 BNSS is sought, precisely because family members named in a matrimonial dispute often learn of a complaint before any arrest is attempted. An anticipatory bail application in a 498A matter typically argues, alongside the general Sibbia/Sushila Aggarwal factors, the specific role attributed to each accused (a distant relative or elderly parent named in a general, undifferentiated list of accused is a materially different case from the husband against whom specific incidents are alleged), the Arnesh Kumar checklist, and the absence of any risk of the accused influencing the complainant or evidence. Because multiple family members are frequently named together, each accused's individual role and the specificity of the allegations against them — not the allegations against the family as a whole — is usually the decisive factor a court weighs.

The Criminal Case and the PWDVA Civil Proceeding Are Not the Same Thing

It is common, and often confusing for families, for a Section 85 BNS criminal complaint and a case under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (PWDVA) to run at the same time, arising from the same set of facts. They are legally distinct:

  • Section 85 BNS is a criminal prosecution. Its purpose is punishment. It is tried before a Magistrate as a criminal case, requires proof beyond reasonable doubt, and can result in imprisonment and fine on conviction.
  • PWDVA is a civil remedy. It is filed before a Magistrate under Section 12 of the Act and seeks protection orders, residence orders, monetary relief, custody arrangements, or compensation — not imprisonment as a primary outcome (though breach of a protection order does carry separate criminal consequences under the Act). The standard of proof and the object of the proceeding are different from a criminal trial.

Defending against one does not automatically dispose of the other, and a strategy built for the criminal complaint is not automatically the right strategy for the PWDVA proceeding — the evidence, the forum-specific procedure, and the practical relief being sought all differ. Where both are filed, they need to be assessed and handled as a coordinated but distinct pair of matters, not as a single case with two names.

Defence Strategy: What Actually Gets Examined

Without commenting on any specific case, the general lines of inquiry in a Section 85 BNS defence typically include:

  • Specificity of allegations — whether dates, incidents, and conduct attributed to each named accused are particularised, or whether the complaint uses identical, general language against every relative named
  • Timeline and delay — when the alleged cruelty is said to have occurred relative to when the complaint was filed, and what (if anything) explains any gap
  • Corroboration — what independent material, if any, supports the allegations beyond the complainant's statement
  • Context of the marital dispute — whether the complaint follows, or coincides with, other matrimonial proceedings such as a divorce or maintenance petition, which is relevant context a court is entitled to consider
  • Individual role — particularly for relatives beyond the husband, whether the complaint actually describes conduct by that specific person or relies on their relationship alone
  • Compliance by the investigating agency — whether the Arnesh Kumar / Section 35 BNSS checklist was followed, which can itself become a ground for relief

POCSO Act Defence in Pune

The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (POCSO) exists to protect children from sexual abuse and exploitation, and Parliament built it accordingly: special courts, in-camera trials, child-friendly evidence procedures, statutory presumptions that shift the burden onto the accused, and some of the most stringent sentencing provisions in Indian criminal law. That severity reflects the seriousness of the harm the Act addresses, and nothing on this page should be read as suggesting otherwise.

That same severity is why an accusation under POCSO — whether well-founded, mistaken, or, in rare cases, false — has to be met with a defence built on real procedural knowledge. Every accused person is entitled to a fair trial and due process; that principle applies to POCSO matters precisely because the consequences of a case going wrong, in either direction, are so serious.

This page explains how a POCSO case proceeds in Pune, the Act's own safeguards, where genuine factual disputes arise, and what a defence lawyer's role involves.

The Special Procedural Framework Under POCSO

POCSO cases are not tried like ordinary criminal cases. The Act builds in safeguards specifically for the child:

  • Special Courts (Section 28) — every case is tried before a Sessions Court designated as a Special Court.
  • In-camera trial (Section 37) — proceedings are private, and the child's identity is protected from disclosure, including a bar on publishing anything that could reveal who the child is.
  • Child-friendly evidence (Sections 33 and 36) — the child need not see the accused while testifying; questions are routed through the Special Court rather than direct cross-examination; statements can be recorded via video-conferencing or at a place of the child's choice.
  • Time-bound trial — evidence recorded within 30 days of cognizance, and trial completed, as far as possible, within one year.

These provisions exist because a trial is itself difficult for a child, and the law reduces that harm without removing the accused's right to a defence.

Where Genuine Factual and Legal Disputes Arise

Not every POCSO case is factually straightforward, and a competent defence has to engage honestly with where real disputes exist.

Age determination. POCSO applies where the person is under 18. Where a birth certificate or school record is unavailable or contested, age is often established through medical assessment (commonly ossification testing), which carries a known margin of error — making genuine age at the relevant time a legitimate, sometimes outcome-determinative issue.

Cases involving a relationship between two young people. A recognised category of POCSO cases involves parties in a consensual relationship where one or both are older teenagers close in age. Because a minor's stated consent is not, in itself, a defence under POCSO, such relationships can fall within the Act's scope without any allegation of coercion — a continuing subject of judicial and legislative discussion in India, including parliamentary recommendations on distinguishing such cases from predatory offences. These matters are litigated strictly on their facts, and the distinction matters to both strategy and sentencing.

The statutory presumptions. Sections 29 and 30 presume culpable mental state and, in defined circumstances, the commission of the offence once the prosecution establishes certain foundational facts — shifting the burden to the accused to rebut that presumption. This is a materially different starting point from ordinary criminal procedure and shapes how a defence is planned.

FIRs shaped by unrelated disputes. A complaint can occasionally arise from or be coloured by a separate dispute — custody, property, or family conflict. Establishing this requires concrete evidence of motive and inconsistency, not assertion.

Bail Under POCSO

POCSO carries no explicit statutory bar on bail comparable to NDPS Section 37, but courts approach bail with considerable caution. Given the gravity the Act attaches to these offences, both Sessions Courts and the Bombay High Court weigh the nature of the allegation, the evidence at that stage, any genuine age dispute, and the risk to the investigation before granting relief. Bail — anticipatory or regular — is rarely routine in a POCSO matter and has to be built on the specific facts.

The Special POCSO Court Process in Pune

Pune has Special Courts designated under Section 28 to try POCSO cases exclusively. A case moves through FIR registration; medical examination and recording of the child's statement under Section 164 BNSS procedure; investigation and charge sheet; framing of charges; in-camera trial; and judgment. Throughout, the defence's role is to test the prosecution's evidence, raise legitimate disputes such as age or the nature of a relationship where they genuinely exist, and hold the state to the presumption-rebuttal standard the Act sets — without obstructing the proceedings' child-protective purpose.

A defence engagement typically covers an unhurried case assessment of the FIR, statement, and medical evidence; a bail strategy addressing the specific concerns a Special Court will have rather than a template submission; evidence planning within the Act's child-protective procedure; and trial representation through to judgment.

NDPS Defence in Pune

A charge under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (NDPS Act) is not an ordinary criminal matter, and it should not be handled with an ordinary criminal defence strategy. The Act is deliberately punitive — it carries some of the harshest bail restrictions in Indian criminal law, mandatory minimum sentences for commercial-quantity offences, and a set of search, seizure, and sampling procedures that, when followed correctly, are hard to dislodge and, when not followed correctly, can unravel the prosecution's entire case. Whether a case is winnable on bail, on procedure, or only at trial depends on facts that need to be examined early — the quantity recovered, how the search was conducted, who witnessed it, and how the seized substance was sampled and forwarded for testing all matter more in an NDPS case than in almost any other criminal matter.

This page explains, in general terms, why NDPS cases are handled differently — not as a substitute for a case-specific consultation, which is essential before any strategy is finalised.

Why NDPS Bail Is Different: Section 37

Bail in an ordinary criminal case asks whether the accused is likely to appear for trial and whether release would interfere with the investigation. Section 37 of the NDPS Act asks something much harder to satisfy. Before a court can grant bail in most NDPS cases (broadly, those not involving small quantities), it must be affirmatively satisfied of two conditions together, not just one:

  1. There are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused is not guilty of the offence, and
  2. There are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused is not likely to commit any offence while on bail.

Both conditions have to be satisfied at the same time. This reverses the usual presumption that runs in favour of liberty at the bail stage — under Section 37, the court has to form a preliminary view of innocence before it can even move to the question of release. This is why NDPS bail applications are rejected far more often than bail applications in other offences, and why an application built on generic grounds ("no prior record," "cooperating with investigation") rarely succeeds here. A Section 37 application has to engage directly with the two conditions — pointing to specific weaknesses in the prosecution's case (on recovery, on procedure, on the quantity actually attributable to the accused) that support a reasonable belief of innocence, and separately addressing the risk of re-offending.

Because of this heightened threshold, an NDPS bail application that has not been built around Section 37 specifically — rather than adapted from a standard bail template — starts at a significant disadvantage.

Section 50: The Search Procedure Safeguard

Section 50 of the NDPS Act gives a person about to be searched (in respect of their person, under specific circumstances) the right to be searched in the presence of a gazetted officer or a magistrate, if they so choose. This is not a technicality — it is a statutory safeguard against planted evidence and coercive search practices, and the Supreme Court has repeatedly treated compliance with Section 50 as mandatory, not directory, in personal search cases where it applies.

In practice, this makes Section 50 one of the most examined issues in NDPS defence:

  • Was the accused actually informed of the right to be searched before a gazetted officer or magistrate?
  • Was that information given in a form the accused could understand, and was consent (or refusal) properly recorded?
  • Was the search conducted by the police officer who informed the accused of the right, or was an independent gazetted officer or magistrate actually involved when requested?

Where the safeguard was not properly extended or documented, it can go to the root of the recovery evidence. This is why a Section 50 compliance review — checking the panchnama, the arrest memo, and the investigating officer's own testimony for internal consistency — is one of the first things worth doing in any NDPS case involving a personal search.

Section 52A: Sampling and Evidence Procedure

Section 52A of the NDPS Act governs how seized narcotic substances are to be inventoried, sampled, and disposed of, including certification of the inventory before a magistrate. Because the seized contraband itself is often destroyed or disposed of well before trial, the integrity of this sampling and documentation procedure is frequently the only real evidence connecting the accused to a specific quantity of a specific substance.

Common defence questions on Section 52A compliance include:

  • Was the inventory prepared and certified before a magistrate in the manner the section requires, and within a reasonable time of seizure?
  • Were samples drawn in the presence of the magistrate, and in a manner that preserves the integrity of the chain of custody?
  • Is there an unexplained or unreasonable gap between seizure and the sampling/certification process — a gap during which the substance and its documentation were in police custody alone?

Gaps or irregularities here do not automatically end a case, but they are a genuine, frequently litigated ground for challenging the reliability of the prosecution's forensic evidence, particularly where the certified sample results are central to establishing the quantity involved.

Quantity Matters More Than in Any Other Offence

The NDPS Act classifies offences by quantity — broadly described in the Act and its notifications as small quantity, intermediate (or "in-between") quantity, and commercial quantity, with the specific threshold varying substance by substance. This classification is not a minor detail; it is the single factor that drives the most consequential outcomes in the case:

  • Sentencing exposure rises sharply as the quantity classification rises, with commercial-quantity offences attracting mandatory minimum sentences and significantly higher maximum sentences than small-quantity offences.
  • Bail difficulty rises correspondingly — the strict twin-condition test under Section 37 applies with full force to commercial-quantity (and, depending on the specific provision, intermediate-quantity) cases, while small-quantity matters are generally dealt with under a more accessible procedure and standard.
  • Which quantity is actually attributable to the accused — especially in cases involving multiple accused, joint recovery, or contested weighment — is itself often a live, disputed issue, not a settled fact.

Because the exact numerical thresholds are fixed by government notification and differ for every scheduled substance, they should be confirmed against the current notification for the specific substance involved in a case rather than assumed. What matters strategically is understanding, early, which classification the prosecution is proceeding on and whether that classification is actually supportable on the recovery as documented.

Defence Strategy: What Actually Gets Examined

An NDPS defence built on a case-specific review typically works through the following, roughly in this order:

  1. The recovery itself — where, how, and from whom the substance was recovered, and whether the version in the FIR and panchnama is internally consistent with the arrest memo and any CCTV or independent witness account available.
  2. Section 50 compliance, where a personal search is involved — whether the right to be searched before a gazetted officer or magistrate was properly communicated and honoured.
  3. Section 52A compliance — the inventory, sampling, and certification trail from seizure to forensic report.
  4. Quantity classification — whether the quantity attributed to the accused is correctly classified as small, intermediate, or commercial, and whether that classification is actually made out on the record.
  5. Bail strategy under Section 37 (or the small-quantity procedure, where applicable) — built around the specific weaknesses identified in steps 1–4, not a generic template.
  6. Trial strategy, where bail is not immediately achievable — focusing on the same procedural and evidentiary issues at the framing-of-charge and evidence stage, and on custody-related safeguards under Section 187 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), which governs police custody and remand periods during investigation.

No two NDPS cases turn on the same combination of these factors, which is why a proper case review — of the FIR, panchnama, arrest memo, and any forensic report available — comes before any strategy is proposed, not after.

In short: A criminal lawyer in Pune advises and appears for a person who is accused of an offence, has received a police notice or has been arrested. The work changes at each stage: before an FIR or notice, at arrest and remand, at bail, after the charge sheet, at trial and on appeal. This page explains each stage, which court in Pune or Mumbai hears it, and what to bring to a first consultation. The office is in Shivajinagar, near the Pune District and Sessions Court.

What a criminal lawyer in Pune does

People search for a criminal lawyer, criminal advocate, crime lawyer or criminal attorney. In Indian courts the person who appears for you is an advocate, enrolled with a State Bar Council. A criminal defence advocate reads the papers, explains the sections and the court, and appears at each hearing.

Advocate Akash R. Chikate is enrolled with the Bar Council of Maharashtra & Goa (MAH/4681/2020) and holds B.A. LL.B. and LL.M. degrees. Consultations are in Marathi, Hindi and English.

Since 1 July 2024 the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) replaces the IPC, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) replaces the CrPC, and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) replaces the Evidence Act. Offences before that date are generally dealt with under the old laws, so the lawyer first checks which code applies. This page gives new and old numbers together. See the CrPC to BNSS and IPC to BNS section table.

What a criminal lawyer does at each stage

Before an FIR, or when a police notice arrives

An FIR is registered under Section 173 BNSS (old Section 154 CrPC). If you think a complaint may be filed against you, you can check whether an FIR is registered. A lawyer helps here in three ways:

  • Police notice. The police may send a notice to appear under Section 35(3) BNSS (old Section 41A CrPC). The lawyer reads it, prepares you for questioning and goes with you where permitted. See police notice under Section 35 BNSS.
  • Protection from arrest. Where arrest is feared, anticipatory bail can be sought under Section 482 BNSS (old Section 438 CrPC) from the Sessions Court or the High Court.
  • Complaint review. If the FIR looks false or exaggerated, the lawyer reviews it. Read about remedies against a false FIR.

The Supreme Court held on 15 January 2026, in Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation, that for offences punishable with up to seven years, a notice under Section 35(3) BNSS is the rule and arrest is an exception. Arrest after a notice must rest on material that was not available when the notice was issued.

Arrest and remand

After arrest, the police must tell the person the grounds of arrest and the right to bail (Section 47 BNSS, old Section 50 CrPC). They must inform a relative or friend (Section 48, old Section 50A). The arrested person may meet an advocate during interrogation (Section 38, old Section 41D).

The person must be produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours (Section 58 BNSS, old Section 57 CrPC). The Magistrate decides on remand under Section 187 BNSS (old Section 167 CrPC): police custody, judicial custody, or release. Police custody is limited to 15 days in total. The lawyer appears at this hearing and checks that the arrest followed the law. See police custody and remand, the difference between police and judicial custody, and your rights when arrested.

Bail

Bail depends on whether the offence is bailable. For a non-bailable offence, a regular bail application is made under Section 480 BNSS (old Section 437 CrPC) before the Magistrate or Section 483 BNSS (old Section 439 CrPC) before the Sessions Court or High Court. See regular bail applications and the bail after arrest guide. Two other routes exist for long custody:

  • Default bail when the investigation is not completed in the period fixed by Section 187 BNSS (old Section 167(2) CrPC): 60 or 90 days, depending on the offence.
  • Undertrial release under Section 479 BNSS (old Section 436A CrPC) after the person has been in custody for one-half of the maximum sentence, or one-third for a first-time offender. It does not apply to offences punishable with death or life imprisonment.

Both are covered on the default bail and undertrial release page. If a Sessions Court refuses bail, read what to do next.

Charge sheet

When the investigation ends, the police file a report in court (Section 193 BNSS, old Section 173 CrPC), commonly called the charge sheet. The accused is entitled to copies of the police report and documents (Section 230 BNSS, old Section 207 CrPC). The lawyer reads every page for gaps, contradictions and sections that do not match the facts. See what happens after a charge sheet.

At this stage a discharge application can be filed. BNSS sets a time limit of 60 days: in a Sessions case from commitment (Section 250, old Section 227 CrPC), and in a warrant case from the supply of documents (Section 262, old Section 239 CrPC).

Trial

If the court frames a charge (Section 251 or 263 BNSS, old Sections 228 and 240 CrPC), the trial begins. The prosecution leads its witnesses, and the defence cross-examines them. The accused is then examined on the evidence against him (Section 351 BNSS, old Section 313 CrPC). The defence may lead its own evidence. The court hears arguments and delivers judgment. Serious offences such as murder are tried by the Sessions Court; see Sessions trial defence.

Appeal

A conviction can be challenged. An appeal against a Magistrate's conviction lies to the Sessions Court. An appeal against a Sessions Judge's conviction lies to the Bombay High Court (Section 415 BNSS, old Section 374 CrPC). The appellant can ask the appeal court to suspend the sentence and grant bail while the appeal is pending (Section 430 BNSS, old Section 389 CrPC). Appeals have short time limits, so see a lawyer promptly. See criminal appeals and suspension of sentence.

content.raw:
In short: Quashing of an FIR means asking the Bombay High Court to cancel the FIR and the case that follows from it. The petition is filed under Section 528 BNSS (old Section 482 CrPC) and, often, Article 226 of the Constitution. It is not routine. The court allows it only where the FIR discloses no offence, the case abuses the process of the court, or a private dispute has genuinely been settled.

What quashing of an FIR means

An FIR starts a police investigation. If the police find enough material, they file a chargesheet and a trial follows. Quashing asks the High Court to stop the case before that point, or at any later stage before the trial ends.

People also search for this as a "quash petition" or "FIR quashing petition". It is the same thing: a petition filed in the High Court asking it to set aside an FIR or a pending criminal case. A step-by-step explanation is in our guide to the quash petition, its grounds, documents and procedure.

The High Court does not decide guilt in a quashing petition. It asks a narrower question: should this case be allowed to continue at all?

Which court can quash an FIR: Bombay High Court at Mumbai

Only the High Court has this power. A Magistrate or a Sessions Court cannot quash an FIR. Section 528 BNSS speaks of "the inherent powers of the High Court".

There is no Pune bench of the Bombay High Court. A quashing petition against an FIR registered in Pune or Pimpri-Chinchwad is heard at the Bombay High Court in Mumbai. The same court hears petitions against FIRs registered in Mumbai.

The office is in Shivajinagar, Pune. Matters before the Bombay High Court and Mumbai courts are handled, and consultation can be by phone or video. For the High Court side of the practice, see Bombay High Court criminal lawyer.

Section 528 BNSS (old Section 482 CrPC) and Article 226

On 1 July 2024 the BNSS replaced the CrPC. Section 482 CrPC became Section 528 BNSS. The wording is the same. Nothing in the Sanhita limits the High Court's inherent powers to make orders that give effect to an order under it, prevent abuse of the process of any court, or secure the ends of justice.

The section does not give the High Court new powers. It saves powers the court already has. The Supreme Court has also said the High Court does not act as an appeal or revision court when it uses them.

Petitions are often filed under both Section 528 BNSS and Article 226. This matters at the chargesheet stage. In a September 2025 order arising from a Bombay High Court petition, the Supreme Court said Article 226 is no longer available once a Magistrate has taken cognisance. Section 528 BNSS can still quash the FIR, the chargesheet and the cognisance order, if that order is on record and a strong case is made out.

FIRs registered before 1 July 2024 are still investigated under the CrPC, so petitions about them may still cite Section 482 CrPC. The legal tests are the same. Our guide to Section 482 CrPC and Section 528 BNSS explains the section in detail, and the CrPC to BNSS table lists other changed numbers.

When FIR quashing is available

A petition can be filed at different stages. The stage changes what the court can look at.

  • After the FIR, during investigation. The court looks mainly at the FIR itself. The Supreme Court has said courts should not stop an investigation at an early stage unless the FIR discloses no offence at all.
  • After the chargesheet. The police report under Section 193 BNSS (old Section 173 CrPC) is also before the court, with the statements and documents. Read our note on what happens after a chargesheet is filed.
  • After a settlement. Where the parties in a private dispute have settled, they can ask the court to quash the case on that basis.
  • Later in the case. A petition can still be filed, but the Sessions Court may be the better place to ask for discharge. See discharge application.

Quashing is not a substitute for bail. If arrest is the main worry, anticipatory bail is a separate and often faster remedy.

Grounds for quashing of FIR: the Bhajan Lal categories

The Supreme Court's decision in State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal (1992 Supp (1) SCC 335) lists seven kinds of cases where an FIR or complaint can be quashed. In plain words:

  1. The allegations, even if fully accepted as true, do not make out any offence.
  2. The FIR and the material with it do not disclose a cognizable offence that justifies a police investigation, unless a Magistrate has ordered one.
  3. The allegations are not disputed, and the evidence collected in support still does not disclose an offence.
  4. The allegations make out only a non-cognizable offence, and police cannot investigate it without a Magistrate's order.
  5. The allegations are so absurd and improbable that no prudent person could find enough ground to proceed.
  6. A law expressly bars the case, or provides its own effective remedy for the grievance.
  7. The case is plainly malicious, filed to take revenge because of a private grudge.

Categories 2 and 4 refer to Sections 156 and 155 CrPC. The BNSS equivalents are Section 175 and Section 174. A petition succeeds only when the facts fit one of these categories. A general statement of innocence does not.

The Supreme Court has also warned that quashing should be exercised sparingly and is the exception, not the rule. In Neeharika Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra (2021), a three-judge bench said the court should not test whether the FIR's allegations are reliable or genuine.

Quashing after a compromise or settlement

Many petitions come from matrimonial and money disputes that have been settled. Examples are a case under Section 85 BNS (old Section 498A IPC), or a cheating or breach-of-trust case under Section 318(4) or 316(2) BNS (old Sections 420 and 406 IPC).

In Gian Singh v. State of Punjab (2012), the Supreme Court held that the High Court can quash a case on settlement even where the offence is not compoundable under Section 320 CrPC (now Section 359 BNSS). Quashing on settlement is not the same as compounding.

The court drew a line. Serious offences such as murder and rape cannot be settled this way. Nor can offences of moral turpitude under special statutes such as the Prevention of Corruption Act. But offences that are mainly civil in flavour can be quashed. The court named civil, commercial, financial, partnership and matrimonial or family disputes, where the wrong is basically to the victim and both sides have settled.

A settlement is not enough by itself. The court checks that it is genuine, that it covers the dispute, and whether continuing the case would serve any purpose. Each case is judged on its own facts.

What a quashing petition contains

The contents are set by the facts of the case, but a petition generally has these parts:

  • The parties, the police station, the FIR number and the offences alleged.
  • A short statement of facts, taken from the FIR and the documents on record.
  • The specific ground for quashing, tied to a recognised category or to the settlement.
  • The orders sought: quashing of the FIR, and of the chargesheet and proceedings where those exist.
  • Annexures: the documents the petition relies on.
  • Where relevant, a request for interim relief while the petition is pending.

The State of Maharashtra is made a respondent, and so is the complainant in most cases. Both are given notice and a chance to reply before the final hearing.

Interim protection while the petition is pending

Many people file a quashing petition hoping the court will also stop their arrest. The Supreme Court has set limits on this.

In Neeharika Infrastructure, the Court said an interim order staying the investigation can be passed only with circumspection, not routinely or mechanically. Normally, while an investigation is in progress and the facts are hazy, the High Court should not pass an order of "no coercive steps". The accused should instead apply for anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC, now Section 482 BNSS.

Where a High Court does grant interim protection, it must give brief reasons and make clear what "no coercive steps" means. So interim protection is possible, but it is not automatic, and it is argued separately from the final question of quashing.

Documents to collect

  • A certified or clear copy of the FIR, with the police station and crime number.
  • The chargesheet and its annexures, if filed.
  • Any police notice under Section 35 BNSS, summons or warrant.
  • All court orders so far: bail orders, remand orders, orders on cognisance.
  • The documents that support your case: agreements, bank records, messages, emails, receipts.
  • For a settlement: the signed settlement or compromise deed, and affidavits from both sides.
  • Your identity and address proof.

If you do not yet have the FIR, see how to check an FIR registered against you in Maharashtra.

How long a quashing petition takes

There is no fixed statutory time for deciding a quashing petition, and no official figure to quote. It depends on the High Court's cause list, replies from the State and complainant, and the stage of the case. Treat any promise of a fixed number of weeks or months with caution.

If the petition is dismissed, the case continues before the trial court. Bail, discharge and trial defence remain open. See sessions trial defence.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Treating quashing as a way to avoid arrest. The court may refuse interim protection, so arrange for bail separately where arrest is a risk.
  • Ignoring police notices. A pending petition does not by itself cancel a notice or summons.
  • Relying on a weak settlement. An unsigned, partial or pressured settlement may not be accepted, and serious offences cannot be settled away.
  • Arguing disputed facts. The court does not hold a mini-trial in a quashing petition. Facts that need evidence belong at trial.
  • Filing without the papers. A petition without the FIR, chargesheet and orders is slow to be heard.

Frequently asked questions

Can an FIR be quashed in the Bombay High Court?

Yes, but only in limited situations. The FIR may disclose no offence, the case may be an abuse of process, or the parties may have settled a private dispute. The Supreme Court treats quashing as the exception, so the High Court looks closely at the facts.

Which court can quash an FIR: Magistrate, Sessions Court or High Court?

Only the High Court. A Magistrate or Sessions Court cannot quash an FIR. They can, at the right stage, refuse to take cognisance or discharge the accused, which is a different remedy.

Is there a Pune bench of the Bombay High Court for quashing?

No. There is no Pune bench. A quashing petition about a Pune or Pimpri-Chinchwad FIR is heard by the Bombay High Court in Mumbai.

What is Section 482 CrPC called now?

It is Section 528 BNSS, in force since 1 July 2024. The wording is the same. People still search for "Section 482 CrPC" and "s 482 CrPC", and older cases and FIRs registered before July 2024 still use that number.

Can an FIR be quashed after both sides settle?

Sometimes. Under Gian Singh, the High Court can quash a case arising from a private civil, commercial or matrimonial dispute after a genuine settlement. It will not do so for serious offences such as murder or rape.

Will the High Court stop my arrest while the quashing petition is pending?

Not automatically. In Neeharika Infrastructure the Supreme Court said such orders should not be passed routinely and that the accused should normally seek anticipatory bail. Whether protection is given depends on the facts and the stage.

Can I file for quashing after the chargesheet is filed?

Yes. A petition can be filed after the chargesheet, and the court may then also look at the police report and documents. In a September 2025 order, the Supreme Court said that filing a chargesheet does not by itself make a petition under Section 528 BNSS pointless. The petition should ask for the right orders, including quashing of the chargesheet and any cognisance order.

How long does an FIR quashing petition take?

There is no fixed time. It depends on the High Court's list, the replies from the State and complainant, and the stage of the case. A reliable estimate is possible only after the papers have been reviewed.

Fees for a quashing petition depend on the court and the stage and are agreed at consultation. See criminal lawyer fees in Pune. If you need advice on your situation, you can contact the office.

Section 528 BNSS (old Section 482 CrPC) and Article 226

On 1 July 2024 the BNSS replaced the CrPC. Section 482 CrPC became Section 528 BNSS. The wording is the same. Nothing in the Sanhita limits the High Court’s inherent powers to make orders that give effect to an order under it, prevent abuse of the process of any court, or secure the ends of justice.

The section does not give the High Court new powers. It saves powers the court already has. The Supreme Court has also said the High Court does not act as an appeal or revision court when it uses them.

Petitions are often filed under both Section 528 BNSS and Article 226. This matters at the chargesheet stage. In a September 2025 order arising from a Bombay High Court petition, the Supreme Court said Article 226 is no longer available once a Magistrate has taken cognisance. Section 528 BNSS can still quash the FIR, the chargesheet and the cognisance order, if that order is on record and a strong case is made out.

FIRs registered before 1 July 2024 are still investigated under the CrPC, so petitions about them may still cite Section 482 CrPC. The legal tests are the same. Our guide to Section 482 CrPC and Section 528 BNSS explains the section in detail, and the CrPC to BNSS table lists other changed numbers.

When FIR quashing is available

A petition can be filed at different stages. The stage changes what the court can look at.

  • After the FIR, during investigation. The court looks mainly at the FIR itself. The Supreme Court has said courts should not stop an investigation at an early stage unless the FIR discloses no offence at all.
  • After the chargesheet. The police report under Section 193 BNSS (old Section 173 CrPC) is also before the court, with the statements and documents. Read our note on what happens after a chargesheet is filed.
  • After a settlement. Where the parties in a private dispute have settled, they can ask the court to quash the case on that basis.
  • Later in the case. A petition can still be filed, but the Sessions Court may be the better place to ask for discharge. See discharge application.

Quashing is not a substitute for bail. If arrest is the main worry, anticipatory bail is a separate and often faster remedy.

Grounds for quashing of FIR: the Bhajan Lal categories

The Supreme Court’s decision in State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal (1992 Supp (1) SCC 335) lists seven kinds of cases where an FIR or complaint can be quashed. In plain words:

  1. The allegations, even if fully accepted as true, do not make out any offence.
  2. The FIR and the material with it do not disclose a cognizable offence that justifies a police investigation, unless a Magistrate has ordered one.
  3. The allegations are not disputed, and the evidence collected in support still does not disclose an offence.
  4. The allegations make out only a non-cognizable offence, and police cannot investigate it without a Magistrate’s order.
  5. The allegations are so absurd and improbable that no prudent person could find enough ground to proceed.
  6. A law expressly bars the case, or provides its own effective remedy for the grievance.
  7. The case is plainly malicious, filed to take revenge because of a private grudge.

Categories 2 and 4 refer to Sections 156 and 155 CrPC. The BNSS equivalents are Section 175 and Section 174. A petition succeeds only when the facts fit one of these categories. A general statement of innocence does not.

The Supreme Court has also warned that quashing should be exercised sparingly and is the exception, not the rule. In Neeharika Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra (2021), a three-judge bench said the court should not test whether the FIR’s allegations are reliable or genuine.

Quashing after a compromise or settlement

Many petitions come from matrimonial and money disputes that have been settled. Examples are a case under Section 85 BNS (old Section 498A IPC), or a cheating or breach-of-trust case under Section 318(4) or 316(2) BNS (old Sections 420 and 406 IPC).

In Gian Singh v. State of Punjab (2012), the Supreme Court held that the High Court can quash a case on settlement even where the offence is not compoundable under Section 320 CrPC (now Section 359 BNSS). Quashing on settlement is not the same as compounding.

The court drew a line. Serious offences such as murder and rape cannot be settled this way. Nor can offences of moral turpitude under special statutes such as the Prevention of Corruption Act. The court named civil, commercial, financial, partnership and matrimonial or family disputes, where the wrong is basically to the victim and both sides have settled.

A settlement is not enough by itself. The court checks that it is genuine, that it covers the dispute, and whether continuing the case would serve any purpose. Each case is judged on its own facts.

What a quashing petition contains

The contents are set by the facts of the case, but a petition generally has these parts:

  • The parties, the police station, the FIR number and the offences alleged.
  • A short statement of facts, taken from the FIR and the documents on record.
  • The specific ground for quashing, tied to a recognised category or to the settlement.
  • The orders sought: quashing of the FIR, and of the chargesheet and proceedings where those exist.
  • Annexures: the documents the petition relies on.
  • Where relevant, a request for interim relief while the petition is pending.

The State of Maharashtra is made a respondent, and so is the complainant in most cases. Both are given notice and a chance to reply before the final hearing.

Interim protection while the petition is pending

Many people file a quashing petition hoping the court will also stop their arrest. The Supreme Court has set limits on this.

In Neeharika Infrastructure, the Court said an interim order staying the investigation can be passed only with circumspection, not routinely or mechanically. Normally, while an investigation is in progress and the facts are hazy, the High Court should not pass an order of “no coercive steps”. The accused should instead apply for anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC, now Section 482 BNSS.

Where a High Court does grant interim protection, it must give brief reasons and make clear what “no coercive steps” means. So interim protection is possible, but it is not automatic, and it is argued separately from the final question of quashing.

Documents to collect

  • A certified or clear copy of the FIR, with the police station and crime number.
  • The chargesheet and its annexures, if filed.
  • Any police notice under Section 35 BNSS, summons or warrant.
  • All court orders so far: bail orders, remand orders, orders on cognisance.
  • The documents that support your case: agreements, bank records, messages, emails, receipts.
  • For a settlement: the signed settlement or compromise deed, and affidavits from both sides.
  • Your identity and address proof.

If you do not yet have the FIR, see how to check an FIR registered against you in Maharashtra.

How long a quashing petition takes

There is no fixed statutory time for deciding a quashing petition, and no official figure to quote. It depends on the High Court’s cause list, replies from the State and complainant, and the stage of the case. Treat any promise of a fixed number of weeks or months with caution.

If the petition is dismissed, the case continues before the trial court. Bail, discharge and trial defence remain open. See sessions trial defence.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Treating quashing as a way to avoid arrest. The court may refuse interim protection, so arrange for bail separately where arrest is a risk.
  • Ignoring police notices. A pending petition does not by itself cancel a notice or summons.
  • Relying on a weak settlement. An unsigned, partial or pressured settlement may not be accepted, and serious offences cannot be settled away.
  • Arguing disputed facts. The court does not hold a mini-trial in a quashing petition. Facts that need evidence belong at trial.
  • Filing without the papers. A petition without the FIR, chargesheet and orders is slow to be heard.

Yes, but only in limited situations. The FIR may disclose no offence, the case may be an abuse of process, or the parties may have settled a private dispute. The Supreme Court treats quashing as the exception, so the High Court looks closely at the facts.

Only the High Court. A Magistrate or Sessions Court cannot quash an FIR. They can, at the right stage, refuse to take cognisance or discharge the accused, which is a different remedy.

Sometimes. Under Gian Singh, the High Court can quash a case arising from a private civil, commercial or matrimonial dispute after a genuine settlement. It will not do so for serious offences such as murder or rape.

Not automatically. In Neeharika Infrastructure the Supreme Court said such orders should not be passed routinely and that the accused should normally seek anticipatory bail. Whether protection is given depends on the facts and the stage.

Yes. A petition can be filed after the chargesheet, and the court may then also look at the police report and documents. In a September 2025 order, the Supreme Court said that filing a chargesheet does not by itself make a petition under Section 528 BNSS pointless. The petition should ask for the right orders, including quashing of the chargesheet and any cognisance order.

How long does an FIR quashing petition take?

There is no fixed time. It depends on the High Court’s list, the replies from the State and complainant, and the stage of the case. A reliable estimate is possible only after the papers have been reviewed.

In short: A bail application asks a court to release a person who is already in custody, on a bond and usually with a surety. A Magistrate decides it under Section 480 BNSS (old Section 437 CrPC). The Sessions Court at Shivajinagar and the Bombay High Court decide it under Section 483 BNSS (old Section 439 CrPC). If the offence is bailable, release is a matter of right. If it is non-bailable, the court weighs the facts.

This page is for families in Pune and Pimpri-Chinchwad whose relative has been arrested. Anticipatory bail (before arrest) is a different remedy: see anticipatory bail in Pune. The office is in Shivajinagar, Pune, near the Pune District and Sessions Court. Matters before the Bombay High Court in Mumbai and Mumbai courts are also handled, with consultation by phone or video.

Bailable and non-bailable offences

Everything starts with one question: is the offence bailable or non-bailable? The First Schedule to the BNSS lists this for each offence (Section 2(1) BNSS defines both terms). Your FIR copy shows the sections applied.

  • Bailable offence: Section 478 BNSS (old Section 436 CrPC) says the person must be released on bail if ready to furnish it. The police officer or the court cannot refuse. If a person cannot give a surety, the court may release an indigent person on a personal bond, and may presume indigence if bail is not furnished within one week of arrest.
  • Non-bailable offence: bail is not a right. The court uses its discretion and records reasons. This is where most bail applications, and most of the work, lie.

Section 479 BNSS (old Section 436A CrPC) separately limits how long an undertrial can stay in jail. It does not apply to offences punishable with death or life imprisonment. See default bail and undertrial release.

Which court, which section

CourtSection (BNSS / old CrPC)What it covers
Police officer or Magistrate478 / 436Bailable offences. Release on bond, with or without surety.
Magistrate (courts other than Sessions and High Court)480 / 437Non-bailable offences. Not if there are reasonable grounds to believe the offence is punishable with death or life imprisonment, with limited exceptions.
Sessions Court, Pune483 / 439Wide power to release an accused in custody, including in offences a Magistrate cannot touch.
Bombay High Court, Mumbai483 / 439Same power. Used after a Sessions Court refusal, or where the law and facts call for it.

There is no Pune bench of the Bombay High Court. High Court bail matters are filed and heard in Mumbai.

For cases registered before 1 July 2024, a court may still refer to the old CrPC numbers. The test for bail is the same, and the sections only renumbered. See the CrPC to BNSS section table.

Bail after arrest and remand: the first days

Under Section 58 BNSS, the police must produce an arrested person before a Magistrate within 24 hours, excluding travel time. The Magistrate then decides remand under Section 187 BNSS (old Section 167 CrPC). The first remand hearing is itself a chance to apply for bail.

  • Police custody can be up to 15 days in total. Under Section 187 BNSS, those days can be taken in parts within the first 40 days (of a 60-day period) or 60 days (of a 90-day period).
  • Section 480(1) BNSS says the need for identification, or for police custody beyond the first 15 days, is not by itself a reason to refuse bail if the accused agrees to follow the court's directions.
  • If the chargesheet is not filed within 60 days (90 days for offences punishable with death, life imprisonment or ten years or more), the accused has a right to default bail, if prepared to furnish bail.

Read more: police custody and remand in Pune.

Section 480 BNSS (old Section 437 CrPC): the Magistrate's power

A Magistrate can grant bail in a non-bailable offence, but Section 480(1) sets limits. Bail is barred where there are reasonable grounds to believe the offence is punishable with death or life imprisonment. The court may still release a child, a woman, or a sick or infirm person. A prior conviction record can also bar bail in cognizable offences. Before granting bail in offences punishable with seven years or more, the Magistrate must hear the Public Prosecutor.

The Magistrate must record reasons for granting bail (Section 480(4)). Under Section 480(6), if a Magistrate's trial is not finished within 60 days from the first date fixed for evidence and the accused has been in custody throughout, the accused should be released on bail, unless the Magistrate records reasons in writing.

Section 483 BNSS (old Section 439 CrPC): Sessions Court and Bombay High Court

Section 483(1) lets the High Court and the Court of Session direct that an accused in custody be released on bail, and set aside or change a condition imposed by a Magistrate. The Section 480 bars on death and life offences do not limit these courts. The Supreme Court said so in Gurcharan Singh v. State (Delhi Administration) (1978) 1 SCC 118. In practice, for offences triable only by the Sessions Court, the Sessions Court is the first stop.

Before granting bail in an offence triable only by the Court of Session, or one punishable with life imprisonment, the court must notify the Public Prosecutor, unless it records that notice is not practicable.

What courts weigh in a non-bailable case

There is no fixed formula. The Supreme Court has said that bail is the rule and jail the exception, that pre-trial detention should not be punishment, and that both the seriousness of the charge and the wider circumstances count (Sanjay Chandra v. CBI, (2012) 1 SCC 40). Courts commonly look at:

  • the nature and gravity of the allegation and the punishment it carries;
  • whether the accused may flee, or has roots in Pune and a fixed address;
  • whether the accused may tamper with evidence or influence witnesses;
  • any earlier cases or convictions;
  • how far the investigation has come, and whether custody is still needed;
  • the time already spent in custody and the likely time for trial.

Bail conditions

For offences punishable with seven years or more, and some other listed offences, Section 480(3) BNSS makes certain conditions compulsory: attend as the bond requires, do not commit a similar offence, do not threaten or induce witnesses, and do not tamper with evidence. The court may add other conditions it thinks necessary. Conditions depend on the case. A Magistrate's conditions can be challenged before the Sessions Court or High Court under Section 483(1)(b). Breaking a condition is a ground to seek cancellation.

Surety and bonds

  • Bond and surety: before release, the person signs a bond for an amount the court considers adequate. If released on a bail bond, one or more suitable sureties are needed (Section 485 BNSS). Any bail condition must be written into the bond.
  • Amount: under Section 484 BNSS the bond amount must have regard to the circumstances and must not be excessive. The High Court or Sessions Court can reduce the amount fixed by a police officer or Magistrate.
  • Fitness of surety: the court may accept affidavits to decide whether a surety is fit and sufficient, or inquire itself.
  • If the accused does not appear: the bond can be forfeited under Section 491 BNSS.

The papers a surety must bring differ from court to court in Pune. Ask the court staff or your advocate before the surety attends. Fees depend on court and stage and are agreed at consultation: see criminal lawyer fees in Pune.

Cancellation of bail

Bail can be cancelled after it is granted. The powers are:

  • Section 480(5) BNSS (old Section 437(5) CrPC): the court that granted bail can order the person arrested and committed to custody.
  • Section 483(3) BNSS (old Section 439(2) CrPC): the High Court or Court of Session can order the same for a person released on bail under this Chapter.

The State usually applies. A complainant can also apply. Courts treat cancellation more strictly than refusing bail at the start. In Dolat Ram v. State of Haryana (1995) 1 SCC 349, the Supreme Court said very cogent and overwhelming circumstances are needed to cancel bail already granted. In Deepak Yadav v. State of U.P. (2022) 8 SCC 559, it said cancellation is not limited to later misconduct: a bail order that is perverse or ignores material facts can also be set aside. Typical grounds are tampering with witnesses, breach of conditions, absconding or a fresh offence. The accused is heard before a decision.

Bail application draft: what it contains

Each court has its own form and numbering for a bail application, sometimes called a criminal miscellaneous bail application. A bail application usually includes:

  • the court, case title and the accused's details;
  • the FIR number, police station, date, sections applied and date of arrest;
  • a short statement of facts and the grounds for bail, one by one;
  • whether an earlier bail application was filed or rejected, and with what result;
  • the prayer, with an offer to follow conditions.

Documents to collect

  • copy of the FIR and arrest memo or intimation;
  • remand order and any earlier bail order;
  • chargesheet or case papers, if filed;
  • identity and address proof of the accused and the proposed surety;
  • medical papers, if health is a ground;
  • proof of employment, family responsibility or settled residence in Pune.

Bail rejected: the next step

A rejection by the Magistrate can be taken to the Sessions Court. A rejection by the Sessions Court can be taken to the Bombay High Court under Section 483 BNSS. A fresh application in the same court usually needs a real change in circumstances, such as a filed chargesheet or longer custody. Read bail rejected by the Sessions Court in Pune: what next and Bombay High Court criminal matters.

How long a court takes depends on the court and its list. The Supreme Court has directed that bail applications should be decided within two weeks unless the law requires otherwise (Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI, (2022) 10 SCC 51), but this is a guideline, not a fixed date. To track a High Court hearing, check the daily cause list on the court's official website.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Filing in the wrong court, or using anticipatory bail after arrest has already happened.
  • Giving a general plea with no dates, documents or address proof.
  • Hiding an earlier rejected application. Courts expect it to be disclosed.
  • Breaking a condition, such as not attending the police station or court.

Frequently asked questions

Jamanat kaise milti hai?

If the offence is bailable, the police or the court must release the person on bail once a bond (and surety if needed) is given. In a non-bailable offence, you apply to the court, which weighs the facts. See jamanat kitne din me milti hai.

What is the difference between Section 437 and Section 439 CrPC?

Section 437 CrPC (now Section 480 BNSS) is the Magistrate's power. Section 439 CrPC (now Section 483 BNSS) belongs to the Sessions Court and High Court, and is wider. Both are explained above.

Which court should file a bail application in Pune?

For bailable offences, the police or Magistrate. For most non-bailable offences, the Magistrate or the Sessions Court at Shivajinagar, depending on the offence. The Bombay High Court is approached after a Sessions Court refusal or where the law allows.

Can the court cancel my bail?

Yes, under Section 480(5) or 483(3) BNSS (old Section 437(5) and 439(2) CrPC). Courts do this for tampering, breach of conditions, absconding or a perverse bail order. They are cautious, and you are heard first.

My bail was rejected. What can I do?

Move the higher court: Sessions Court after a Magistrate, and Bombay High Court after a Sessions Court. A new application in the same court needs changed circumstances. See the guide linked above.

Does a surety have to be from Pune?

The law does not fix this in Section 485 BNSS, which asks that sureties be suitable. Courts decide fitness case by case, and practice varies. Ask the court or your advocate before arranging one.

Where do I see the High Court bail list?

The Bombay High Court publishes daily cause lists, the list of matters to be heard, on its official website. An advocate can confirm the court number and time for a bail matter.

Is bail possible if the police need more custody?

Yes. Under Section 480(1) BNSS, the need for police custody beyond the first 15 days is not by itself a reason to refuse bail, if the accused agrees to follow the court's directions.

Normally you ask for bail after arrest. Anticipatory bail works the other way round. You ask the court in advance, because you have reason to believe you may be arrested for a non-bailable offence.

If the court grants it, the arrest does not lead to jail. The police can still arrest you, but you must be released on bail on the terms the court has set.

It does not cancel the FIR and it does not stop the investigation. You remain an accused until the case ends or is quashed. For a bailable offence, bail is a right at the police station, so this order is usually not needed.

Section 482 BNSS (old Section 438 CrPC)

The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure on 1 July 2024. Anticipatory bail is now in Section 482 BNSS. The old number was Section 438 CrPC, which is why many people still search for "anticipatory bail CrPC" or "sec 438 of CrPC".

The core wording is the same. A person who has reason to believe he may be arrested on an accusation of a non-bailable offence can apply to the High Court or the Court of Session. Offences from before 1 July 2024 are still dealt with under the old laws, so an older FIR may still quote IPC sections. See our CrPC to BNSS section table for old and new numbers.

For step-by-step practical detail, read how to get anticipatory bail in Pune.

Who can apply, and when

The Supreme Court has said that the fear of arrest must rest on real facts, not on a vague worry. An FIR is not required. You can apply before an FIR if the facts clearly show why you expect to be arrested. You can also apply after an FIR, as long as you have not been arrested.

Anticipatory bail is usually considered in situations like these:

  • An FIR has been registered and you are named as an accused.
  • You have received a police notice under Section 35(3) BNSS (old Section 41A CrPC) and fear arrest after questioning.

  • The police have visited your home or workplace, or have called your family, in connection with a case.

Section 482 gives both courts the power to grant anticipatory bail.

  • Pune District and Sessions Court (Shivajinagar): most applicants start here. The court that has jurisdiction depends on where the case is registered.
  • Bombay High Court, Mumbai: this is the High Court for Pune. There is no Pune bench. Applicants usually go here after the Sessions Court refuses, or where the case calls for it. See Bombay High Court criminal lawyer.

Anticipatory bail procedure: the stages

  3. Interim protection. The court may issue notice to the Public Prosecutor and, if it thinks fit, give short-term protection from arrest until the final hearing. This is called interim anticipatory bail. It is not automatic.
  4. Hearing. The Public Prosecutor, usually with inputs from the investigating officer, opposes or responds. The court hears you and decides.
  5. Order. The court grants the application with conditions, or refuses it. If granted, the order applies if you are arrested. You may be asked to furnish a bond, with or without sureties.

What an application contains

The Supreme Court has said that an anticipatory bail application should state the essential facts of the offence, why the applicant reasonably fears arrest, and the applicant's version of events. A general plea such as "I may be falsely implicated sometime" is not enough.

In general, a good application covers these points:

  • The FIR or complaint, or the facts that make arrest likely.
  • The sections alleged and why they are non-bailable.
  • Your role as alleged, and your answer to it.
  • Whether you are cooperating with the police, including any notice received.
  • Your address, work and family ties, which bear on the risk of absconding.
  • Whether you have any earlier case, and whether any earlier bail application was made.
  • The conditions you are ready to accept.

What the court considers

Anticipatory bail is a matter of the court's discretion. In Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab (1980), a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court said that courts weigh several things. These include the nature and seriousness of the accusation, the context of the events, the chance that the applicant will not be available for trial, and the risk that witnesses will be tampered with. The Court also said that if the accusation seems aimed at humiliating the applicant through arrest, bail would generally be granted.

In Sushila Aggarwal v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2020), another Constitution Bench said courts should look at the nature and gravity of the offence, the role of the applicant, the chance of influencing the investigation or tampering with evidence, and the chance of fleeing justice.

Typical conditions

Section 482(2) BNSS lets the court attach conditions suited to the case. The section lists these:

  • Make yourself available for questioning by the police when required.
  • Do not threaten, induce or make promises to anyone who knows the facts, so as to stop them telling the court or the police.
  • Do not leave India without the court's permission.
  • Other conditions that a court can impose on bail under Section 480(3) BNSS. These include attending court as per the bond, not committing a similar offence, and not tampering with evidence.

The police can ask the court to cancel the protection if you break a condition, for example by not cooperating or by threatening witnesses. Read chargesheet filed: what next for the stage after investigation.

  • Copy of the FIR, complaint or police notice, if you have it.
  • Your identity and address proof.
  • Papers that support your side, such as messages, agreements, bank records or medical records.
  • Details and orders of any earlier case or bail application.
  • Names and addresses of possible sureties and their identity papers.

A refusal is not the end of the road. You can apply to the Bombay High Court in Mumbai, which also has power under Section 482. The High Court looks at the Sessions Court's reasons and the facts again. Read bail rejected by the Sessions Court: what next.

If you are arrested in the meantime, regular bail is the remedy. Do not ignore a court date or a police notice while you wait.

  • Waiting until the police are at the door. Plan the application early.
  • Skipping a notice under Section 35(3) BNSS. The notice must be followed. See police notice under Section 35 BNSS.
  • Using a downloaded format that does not match your FIR.
  • Leaving out facts, such as an earlier case, that the other side will raise.
  • Breaking a condition after bail is granted. This can lead to cancellation.
  • Contacting the complainant or witnesses to "settle" matters while the case is pending.
